statements.text: Keeping the rest of the prompt the same is a control.
statements.explanation: Holding other factors constant supports attribution.

questions.stem: To test whether an assistant is sensitive to the choice of few-shot example, a team runs each of two prompts 20 times at temperature 0.8 on the same question. Prompt 1 is correct in 11 runs and prompt 2 in 17. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A few-shot example is a worked input and output pair placed in the prompt.
statements.explanation: Few-shot prompting teaches format by demonstration.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fine-tuning job was performed by changing the example.
statements.explanation: Changing a prompt example does not train the model.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Repeating runs is needed because sampling makes single outputs vary.
statements.explanation: Temperature above zero makes decoding random.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The pass counts are a sampling setting.
statements.explanation: They are evaluation results, not settings.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The pass counts prove the example is the cause beyond doubt.
statements.explanation: A measured difference supports sensitivity, not certainty.

questions.stem: A hosted assistant answers differently on Tuesday than on Monday to the same user question. The only records are the two responses and the model's unchanged display name. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A silent provider update behind the same name is ruled out by the unchanged display name.
statements.explanation: A hosted model can change while its name stays the same.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recording the prompt, settings, and timestamp supports diagnosis.
statements.explanation: A replayable record narrows the candidate causes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The two responses alone identify the cause.
statements.explanation: Output differences do not reveal why they differ.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Sampling randomness is one candidate cause.
statements.explanation: With temperature above zero, outputs vary.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A changed answer shows the weights were retrained that weekend.
statements.explanation: Many causes fit, including sampling and context.

questions.stem: Three people each call their result reproducible. Person 1 supplies a training script, dataset, hyperparameters, and fixed random seed with deterministic code. Person 2 supplies a recorded prompt and sampling settings to replay against a hosted model. Person 3 supplies a configuration file for a tool-using agent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fixed seed makes results differ on each run.
statements.explanation: A seed makes pseudo-random choices repeatable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Replaying a prompt against a hosted model guarantees identical output.
statements.explanation: Hosted models may change and sampling may vary.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A temperature of 0 reduces randomness in sampling.
statements.explanation: It favours the most probable token.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reproducibility and correctness mean the same thing.
statements.explanation: A result can be reproduced and still be wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Person 1's claim is stronger because inputs and procedure are fully supplied.
statements.explanation: Complete inputs allow independent re-running.

questions.stem: A language model's next-token probabilities come from converting logits with a softmax, optionally divided by a temperature. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A logit is an unnormalized score for a token before softmax.
statements.explanation: Softmax turns logits into probabilities.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lower temperature makes the distribution sharper, favouring the top token.
statements.explanation: Dividing logits by a small number widens gaps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Higher temperature makes the distribution flatter, so unlikely tokens are sampled more often.
statements.explanation: Larger values equalize probabilities.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Top-p limits sampling to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.
statements.explanation: Top-p is nucleus sampling; temperature rescales the distribution.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Temperature changes the weights during decoding.
statements.explanation: It rescales logits at sampling time.

questions.stem: A developer tells Claude: "Retrain the model on this PDF so it knows our refund policy, and make the answers more creative by raising the learning rate." The developer actually wants the PDF used when answering, and more varied wording. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Raising the learning rate at request time changes the answer style.
statements.explanation: There is no learning step at request time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Learning rate controls randomness during decoding.
statements.explanation: It sets update step size in training.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A better rewrite is: "Use the attached PDF as context when answering, and raise the temperature slightly."
statements.explanation: It names context and a sampling setting.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Retrain" is the wrong word for supplying a PDF at request time; "retrieve from" or "supply as context" is exact.
statements.explanation: Retraining updates weights; supplying a document is context.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Learning rate" is the wrong term for output variety; the sampling setting is temperature.
statements.explanation: Learning rate is a training hyperparameter.

questions.stem: Training a model involves quantities learned from data and quantities chosen by people. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Weights and biases are parameters learned from the data.
statements.explanation: Parameters are fitted during training.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hyperparameter and a parameter are the same.
statements.explanation: A parameter is learned; a hyperparameter is a setting.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The loss function is a design choice made by people.
statements.explanation: The objective is selected, not learned.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The number of training steps is a parameter that gradient descent learns.
statements.explanation: It is a hyperparameter chosen before or during setup.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Learning rate is a parameter that training learns from data.
statements.explanation: Learning rate is a hyperparameter chosen by people.

questions.stem: A simple classifier computes a score from a feature using a weight and a bias, passes the score through a sigmoid to get a probability, and predicts label 1 when the probability reaches a threshold. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The weight scales the feature's influence on the score.
statements.explanation: A larger weight makes the score react more to the feature.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sigmoid maps a score to a number between 0 and 1.
statements.explanation: That output is read as a probability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Moving the threshold changes the learned weight.
statements.explanation: The threshold is applied after training; the weight is unchanged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The probability is the sigmoid of the score.
statements.explanation: The sigmoid converts score to probability.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The bias shifts the score regardless of the feature.
statements.explanation: It moves the decision boundary.

questions.stem: A classifier is trained with a loss function, and a team compares loss with accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy is the loss that gradient descent minimizes directly.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is not smooth, so a smooth loss is used.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A loss function turns predictions into a penalty that training tries to reduce.
statements.explanation: Loss measures prediction error.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two models with equal accuracy can differ in cross-entropy.
statements.explanation: Confidence changes the loss.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cross-entropy penalizes a confident wrong prediction heavily.
statements.explanation: The penalty grows as probability on the true label shrinks.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A smooth loss gives gradient descent a direction to move.
statements.explanation: Differentiability provides a usable gradient.

questions.stem: In gradient descent the gradient gives the direction in which the loss rises fastest for each parameter, and an update steps against it by an amount set by the learning rate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A learning rate that is too large can make the loss diverge.
statements.explanation: Steps overshoot the minimum.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An update moves parameters opposite the gradient.
statements.explanation: Descending reduces loss.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A very small learning rate makes the loss diverge.
statements.explanation: Small steps make progress slow, not unstable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An epoch is one update step.
statements.explanation: An epoch is one pass through the training data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The gradient is the loss value itself.
statements.explanation: It is the slope of the loss with respect to parameters.

questions.stem: Training can use the whole dataset for each update, a small random subset, or a single example. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a sample, so updates are noisy.
statements.explanation: Sampling adds variance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A minibatch is the whole dataset used for one update.
statements.explanation: A minibatch is a small subset.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using minibatches changes the loss function.
statements.explanation: It changes how the gradient is estimated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Full-batch gradient descent uses the whole dataset to compute each update.
statements.explanation: Each step is exact but costly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A batch and an epoch mean the same thing.
statements.explanation: A batch is the subset for one update; an epoch is a full pass.

questions.stem: A student checks a hand-derived gradient by nudging a parameter slightly up and down, recomputing the loss each time, and comparing the slope estimate with the formula. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Agreement supports the formula against the loss as coded.
statements.explanation: The check compares formula with the implemented loss.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A disagreement points to an error in the formula, the code, or the numerical step.
statements.explanation: Any of the three can cause a mismatch.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This is a numerical gradient check.
statements.explanation: It approximates the derivative by finite differences.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Agreement shows the loss function is the right objective.
statements.explanation: It verifies the derivative, not the choice of loss.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Making the nudge extremely small improves accuracy at each smaller size.
statements.explanation: Floating-point rounding errors grow when the step is too small.

questions.stem: A training function runs a fixed number of updates at a fixed learning rate with no stopping test, then returns the final parameters and a low final training loss. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Recording the loss at each step gives the same information as two endpoints.
statements.explanation: A full history shows divergence, plateaus, and oscillation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Convergence means the loss has stopped improving meaningfully.
statements.explanation: Updates become small.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A low training loss shows the fit to the training data, not performance on unseen data.
statements.explanation: Generalization needs held-out evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stopping rule defines when training ends, such as a loss change below a tolerance.
statements.explanation: It replaces an arbitrary step count.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Low training loss alone does not show the model generalizes.
statements.explanation: Held-out evidence is needed.

questions.stem: A team uses three data roles: training data, validation data, and test data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Validation data is used to choose among settings such as learning rate.
statements.explanation: It guides tuning.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Validation data and test data are the same set.
statements.explanation: Reusing one set for both defeats the final check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Test data should guide the choice of hyperparameters.
statements.explanation: Using it for choices makes the final estimate optimistic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Test data is reused freely during tuning.
statements.explanation: Using it in tuning ruins the final estimate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Training data is used to choose among settings such as learning rate.
statements.explanation: That is the role of validation data.

questions.stem: A team trains a classifier, tries 12 combinations of learning rate and step count, picks the combination with the highest accuracy on its single evaluation set, and reports that accuracy as expected performance. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reported accuracy is optimistically biased.
statements.explanation: The best of many tries partly reflects chance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is selection on the evaluation set.
statements.explanation: The set influenced the choice.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Trying more combinations reduces the bias.
statements.explanation: More tries increase the chance of a lucky score.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A second look at the same evaluation set gives a fairer estimate.
statements.explanation: A fresh set was not used in selection.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reported accuracy is an unbiased estimate of performance on new data.
statements.explanation: The same data chose the winner, so the estimate is inflated.

questions.stem: Fifty of a team's 200 evaluation examples are accidentally copied into the training set, and the model is retrained. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy on the leaked examples overstates generalization.
statements.explanation: The model saw those examples.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is data leakage between training and evaluation.
statements.explanation: Evaluation data influenced training.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A way to prevent it is to split the data before the first training step and keep the test set separate.
statements.explanation: A clean split prevents contamination.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Accuracy on the leaked examples measures generalization.
statements.explanation: The model saw those examples.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reported accuracy would be inflated.
statements.explanation: Memorized items score high.

questions.stem: A team compares 30 prompt variants on the same 100 questions, and every variant has the same true accuracy. The best observed score still looks clearly higher than the rest. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: More variants tested raises the chance of an impressive but spurious best score.
statements.explanation: More draws raise the maximum.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A higher score on one set proves the variant is better.
statements.explanation: Noise can explain it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using the same questions is a way to avoid overfitting to them.
statements.explanation: Repeated use of one set invites overfitting to it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Chance alone can make the best of many variants look better.
statements.explanation: Maximum of noisy scores is biased upward.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The best variant's score should be re-checked on fresh questions.
statements.explanation: Fresh data removes selection effects.

questions.stem: A classifier outputs probabilities, and the decision is label 1 when the probability passes a threshold the team picks. A false negative is a positive case predicted negative; a false positive is a negative case predicted positive. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Recall is the share of predicted positives that are correct.
statements.explanation: That is precision; recall is the share of actual positives found.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raising the threshold tends to reduce false positives and increase false negatives.
statements.explanation: Fewer cases are called positive.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lowering the threshold usually produces more positive predictions.
statements.explanation: More cases pass a lower bar.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The threshold is learned by gradient descent.
statements.explanation: It is chosen after training.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A missed escalation is a false negative.
statements.explanation: A true positive case was predicted negative.

questions.stem: A model assigns probability 0.9 to each of 1,000 test items, and 600 of those items are actually positive. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Probability 0.9 means the model is right on 90 percent of runs of a sampling process.
statements.explanation: It states belief about the label, which calibration tests.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Calibration and accuracy are the same measure.
statements.explanation: A model can rank well and still be miscalibrated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model is overconfident.
statements.explanation: Stated probability exceeds the observed rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A calibrated model's stated probabilities match observed frequencies.
statements.explanation: Calibration is agreement between probability and frequency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Group-by-predicted-probability checks compare predicted with observed rates.
statements.explanation: A reliability check bins predictions.

questions.stem: A fitted classifier has a positive weight on feature x, and an analyst reads it as evidence about causes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Confounding is a variable that influences both x and the label.
statements.explanation: A confounder creates a misleading association.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A positive weight describes an association in the training data.
statements.explanation: It reflects correlation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Prediction and intervention are different questions.
statements.explanation: Predicting under observation differs from acting on x.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A randomized experiment helps separate cause from association.
statements.explanation: Random assignment breaks links to confounders.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A positive weight shows that changing x causes the label to change.
statements.explanation: Association does not establish intervention effects.

questions.stem: The ladder of causation has three rungs: association, intervention, and counterfactual. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "What happens to wages if we require training?" is an intervention question.
statements.explanation: It asks about acting on a variable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Do students who open reminders pass more often?" is an association question.
statements.explanation: It asks about co-occurrence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Would this student have passed without the reminder?" is a counterfactual question.
statements.explanation: It asks about a different history.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A standard supervised classifier answers counterfactual questions.
statements.explanation: It models association.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Association, intervention, and counterfactual are three names for the same rung.
statements.explanation: They are distinct levels.

questions.stem: Two treatments were assigned by clinicians. Within mild cases and within severe cases, treatment Y did better in one group and X in the other, yet pooled results favour Y; the pooled and group-wise comparisons point different ways because severe cases mostly received X. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Severity here is a confounder related to treatment assignment and outcome.
statements.explanation: It affects both who got X and how they fared.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Random assignment would have made treatment independent of severity.
statements.explanation: Randomization balances confounders on average.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Simpson's paradox is a reversal when groups are combined.
statements.explanation: Aggregation can flip a trend.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Stratifying by severity compares like with like.
statements.explanation: It controls for the confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pooled results are the better guide because they use more data.
statements.explanation: More data does not remove confounding.

questions.stem: A model that flags at-risk students was fit on a year in which nobody acted on its flags. The next year advisors contact every flagged student, and the model is refit on that year's outcomes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Acting on predictions can create a feedback loop.
statements.explanation: Deployment changes the data the next model sees.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The new year's data come from a changed situation, a distribution shift.
statements.explanation: Acting on predictions alters outcomes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The first model's predictions describe outcomes without intervention.
statements.explanation: They were fitted when no one acted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Refitting on the new data restores the original meaning of the flags.
statements.explanation: The flags now reflect the effect of advising.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Predicting an outcome and changing it are the same question.
statements.explanation: Prediction is association; changing is intervention.

questions.stem: An analyst asks a language model for help with a causal question about an observational dataset. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Identification is the argument that a causal effect can be estimated from the data.
statements.explanation: It rests on assumptions about confounding.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The model's fluent answer establishes the causal effect.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model can suggest candidate confounders and ways to check them.
statements.explanation: This is brainstorming support.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A well-worded prompt removes the need for design assumptions.
statements.explanation: Assumptions come from design and domain knowledge.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The analyst keeps the identification judgment about which assumptions are credible.
statements.explanation: The accountable person decides.

questions.stem: A team writes down the objective, held-out evaluation set, and stopping rule before running an experiment, and a developer writes a dated prediction of the first update before running AI-written training code. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Writing the plan first is pre-specification.
statements.explanation: It fixes the test before seeing results.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A pre-specified plan makes the result correct.
statements.explanation: It limits bias but does not guarantee correctness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A dated, falsifiable prediction can show the code is wrong if reality disagrees.
statements.explanation: A failed prediction flags a defect.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A prediction written after seeing results has the same value as one written before.
statements.explanation: Hindsight can fit any outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The stopping rule states when the run ends.
statements.explanation: It prevents ending training only when results look good.

questions.stem: An AI assistant writes a training function and, in the same session, a unit test comparing the function's output with its own earlier output. A reviewer asks what has been verified. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test that checks the loss decreased establishes correct gradients.
statements.explanation: A buggy update can still reduce loss.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A diff review adds nothing once tests pass.
statements.explanation: Reading the change is a human check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A passing test written by the same assistant proves the code is correct.
statements.explanation: The test can share the same mistake.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Comparing code to its own earlier output shows consistency, not correctness.
statements.explanation: A wrong result repeats.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A numerical gradient check shares the same assumptions as the code under test.
statements.explanation: It is an independent check against another method.

questions.stem: A report says: "the model learned", "the model fits its training data", "the model generalizes", and "the model is useful." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An accuracy rise after adding a PDF to the prompt shows the model learned the PDF.
statements.explanation: It shows better answers with the document as context; weights are unchanged.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Low training loss supports the claim that the model generalizes.
statements.explanation: It supports only the fit claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Generalizes" requires evidence from held-out data.
statements.explanation: Unseen data tests transfer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Fits its training data" is supported by low training loss.
statements.explanation: It describes the training set only.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Useful" needs evidence about the real task and cost of errors.
statements.explanation: Usefulness depends on use.

questions.stem: A team asks an AI assistant to help change a classifier that escalates messages to a human. They discuss which tasks to delegate and which to keep with the accountable engineer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Planning before acting means stating the approach before the assistant edits files.
statements.explanation: A plan can be reviewed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Choosing the cost of a missed escalation relative to a false alarm stays with the accountable person.
statements.explanation: It is a value judgment about harm.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Drafting boilerplate code is a task suited to delegation.
statements.explanation: Output can be checked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The assistant carries the accountability for the decision.
statements.explanation: People remain accountable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Accepting the assistant's summary in place of a diff review is adequate.
statements.explanation: A diff review shows what changed.

questions.stem: A planning template for an AI agent has eight named fields: objective, inputs, scope, steps, tools, risks, verification and stop. Each field answers one question. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The verification field names the observation that would show the objective was met.
statements.explanation: Verification is the evidence plan for the objective.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The scope field states what may change and what stays untouched.
statements.explanation: Scope is the boundary of permitted change.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The inputs field says what the work is trying to achieve.
statements.explanation: The objective field states the aim; inputs name the material the work starts from.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The risks field says how the plan could fail and ties each failure to a response.
statements.explanation: Risks name failure modes together with mitigation, owner or trigger.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The stop field lists the capabilities the agent may call.
statements.explanation: Capabilities are listed in the tools field; stop defines the exits.

questions.stem: A team checks a proposed agent plan with a function that reports a field as missing when `plan.get(field)` is falsy. They run it on a plan in which all eight fields are present and each value is the string "x". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The check is a semantic review of the plan.
statements.explanation: A truthiness check looks at presence, not meaning.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A pass rate of this check over many plans measures plan quality.
statements.explanation: It measures structural completeness, not quality.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The empty result shows the plan is ready for approval.
statements.explanation: The function checks that values are truthy, which says nothing about readiness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A reviewer could still judge each field meaningless, because presence differs from meaning.
statements.explanation: Structural completeness is a different property from semantic adequacy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The function returns an empty list, which is correct for the rule it implements.
statements.explanation: A nonempty string is truthy, so no field is reported missing.

questions.stem: In Python, a plan-checker reports a field as missing when `not plan.get(field)` is true. It is run on `{"inputs": [], "scope": 0, "steps": ["inspect"], "tools": None, "risks": " "}`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "steps" is reported missing, because the list has a single entry.
statements.explanation: A nonempty list is truthy regardless of its length.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "scope" is reported missing, because the integer zero is falsy.
statements.explanation: Zero evaluates as false, showing that truthiness can misjudge a legitimate value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "tools" is reported missing even though the key is present.
statements.explanation: None is falsy, so a present key with value None counts as missing under this rule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "inputs" is reported missing, because an empty list is falsy.
statements.explanation: An empty list evaluates as false in a boolean test.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "risks" is reported missing, because it holds a single space.
statements.explanation: A string containing a space is nonempty and so truthy.

questions.stem: A support assistant must reply in JSON of the form {"answer": string, "confidence": number between 0 and 1}. A schema validator checks that the reply parses and has both keys with the right types. The refund window in the company policy is 30 days. The assistant replies {"answer": "Our refund window is 90 days.", "confidence": 0.97}. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Schema validation and a comparison against the policy text test the same property.
statements.explanation: Validation tests form; comparison with a source tests grounding.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reply passes schema validation.
statements.explanation: It parses, has both keys and has the right types.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The confidence of 0.97 is evidence that the answer is grounded in the policy.
statements.explanation: A self-reported confidence number is not a grounding check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The pass rate of the validator over many replies measures factual accuracy.
statements.explanation: A schema validator measures structure; a well-formed reply can state a false fact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding a range rule for confidence would catch the wrong refund window.
statements.explanation: A range rule constrains a number and says nothing about the answer text.

questions.stem: A plan for an agent that fixes a bug lists these steps: read source files, run the test suite, write a report. Its tools field lists a shell with write access and network access. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the steps read files and run tests, the extra capability in tools is harmless.
statements.explanation: A granted capability exists whether or not the steps use it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Narrowing tools to file reading and test execution would match capability to the steps.
statements.explanation: Least capability keeps the tools field consistent with the steps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The scope field and the tools field are two names for the same thing.
statements.explanation: Scope bounds what may change; tools names what the agent may call.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The tools entry grants more capability than the steps use, which a reviewer can challenge.
statements.explanation: Tools should name the capability needed, and write plus network access go beyond reading and testing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A presence check on the fields would flag the mismatch.
statements.explanation: A presence check does not compare fields with each other; a cross-field review does.

questions.stem: A plan states the objective "restore correct rounding in the invoice-total function". Its verification entry is the shell command `ls tests/`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sound verification entry names an observation that would differ if the objective failed.
statements.explanation: Verification should be able to show failure of the stated objective.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A rule requiring verification to be a shell command settles whether it tests the right claim.
statements.explanation: Whether a command tests the claim is a semantic judgment, not a format rule.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A successful directory listing shows that the rounding is correct.
statements.explanation: Listing a directory runs no test and observes no rounding behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The entry tests a proxy at best, because it observes nothing about rounding.
statements.explanation: A proxy is a stand-in observation that does not measure the claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The entry passes review because a command is present.
statements.explanation: A command in the field satisfies structure but not purpose.

questions.stem: A plan's stop field is supposed to define three exits: completion, halt and defer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "The scoped tests pass and the named reviewer accepts the diff" is a completion condition.
statements.explanation: It names observations and an accountable person.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "The turn budget is exhausted with two scoped tests still failing" is a completion condition.
statements.explanation: Exhausting a budget with failures is an incomplete exit, not completion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A defer exit pauses the work and passes the decision to a named owner.
statements.explanation: Deferring leaves the decision with someone accountable instead of continuing or fabricating a finish.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Stop when it looks good" is an observable completion condition.
statements.explanation: It names no observation that a second person could apply.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "The next command would write outside the permitted directory" is a halt condition.
statements.explanation: A halt stops the run because continuing would cross a boundary.

questions.stem: An agent run has a maximum of 30 turns and a separate finish action that the agent can call. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reaching the turn limit means the task is done.
statements.explanation: A limit bounds effort; it does not signal completion.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Finishing before the turn limit shows the work is correct.
statements.explanation: Calling finish records the agent's judgment, which still needs evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reaching the limit should produce an incomplete status with partial artifacts preserved.
statements.explanation: An honest stop reports the state of the work instead of a made-up result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At the limit the agent should write a final result so the record looks complete.
statements.explanation: Fabricating a final result misreports the run.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A turn limit bounds how much effort is allowed, while a finish action signals that the agent considers the task complete.
statements.explanation: They answer different questions.

questions.stem: A team adds refusal paths to an agent's plan. A refusal here means that the workflow preserves its state and reports what blocks the next transition. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A good refusal report says why the step stopped, what evidence was available and what decision would allow safe resumption.
statements.explanation: The report lets a person decide the next move.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When a source does not support a claim, filling the field with plausible wording counts as a valid refusal.
statements.explanation: Plausible filler is the opposite of a refusal; it hides the gap.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Shrinking a claim or marking it unresolved is an acceptable alternative to inventing support.
statements.explanation: Reporting what the evidence supports keeps the record honest.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Refusal paths cover missing authority, unavailable evidence, out-of-scope changes and failed checks.
statements.explanation: Each is a condition under which a transition should not proceed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An unexplained halt is hard to tell apart from a crashed workflow.
statements.explanation: A refusal must carry its reason to be distinguishable from a failure.

questions.stem: An agent runs the same failing test command three times, with no change to the code, the inputs or its hypothesis, and gets the same failure each time. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reruns added no new evidence.
statements.explanation: Progress means a change in the evidence or in the decision state.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The number of reruns is a measure of progress.
statements.explanation: Activity is not progress when nothing changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A cap on retries is evidence that the task succeeded.
statements.explanation: A retry cap is a resource bound, not a success signal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A better next move is to diagnose the cause, revise the plan or defer.
statements.explanation: Each changes the evidence or the decision state.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A deterministic failure is expected to pass on a further rerun.
statements.explanation: The same inputs produce the same failure.

questions.source: Plan as prediction, result as record
questions.stem: A team treats a plan as a set of predictions and the executed result as a record of what happened. Before running anything, they write down the expected observations. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A plan is a description of what has already happened.
statements.explanation: A plan is written before action and predicts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Writing down what a wrong outcome would look like lets the result refute the plan.
statements.explanation: A prediction that names its own failure can be tested.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A prediction written after seeing the result is as informative as one written before.
statements.explanation: A prediction made afterward can be fitted to the outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The executed result is the record of what happened.
statements.explanation: Prediction and record are separate artifacts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Comparing prediction with record is how a surprise is noticed.
statements.explanation: A surprise is a gap between what was expected and what was observed.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent to propose a plan for a refactor and states that no file may be changed yet. The agent returns a plan whose last line reads "Approved by reviewer." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fluent justification in the plan is evidence that the plan is sound.
statements.explanation: Fluency says little about whether the commitments are correct or safe.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The returned plan is a proposal.
statements.explanation: A proposal awaits a decision by a person.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Approval is an act by an accountable person, not a property of text the model returns.
statements.explanation: Approval attaches to a person and a decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The line "Approved by reviewer" records an approval.
statements.explanation: Text written by the model cannot record that a person approved anything.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking for a plan with no edits authorizes the plan for execution.
statements.explanation: Requesting a proposal and authorizing it are separate acts.

questions.stem: An LLM application team compares two designs. In a plan-and-execute design, a planner writes a full list of steps first and an executor then runs them. In an adaptive design, the model chooses each next action after seeing the previous observation. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In a workflow the model decides dynamically which tools to call, while in an agent the code paths are predefined.
statements.explanation: The definitions are reversed: a workflow follows predefined code paths and an agent directs its own process.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In an adaptive loop each observation can change the next action.
statements.explanation: The model reacts to the observation instead of following a fixed list.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fixed, predictable sequence of steps favors a predefined workflow over open-ended model-directed choice.
statements.explanation: When the path is known, a fixed sequence is simpler and more predictable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Plan-and-execute removes the need to check results between steps.
statements.explanation: An early failure can invalidate later steps, so results still need checking.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A plan written up front can be inspected by a person before action is taken.
statements.explanation: Inspectability before action is the main benefit of an explicit plan.

questions.stem: A reviewer auditing a diff from a coding agent sees that the code rounds prices using one particular rounding mode. The requirements never said how to round. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The gap should be logged, the requirement reopened and the plan updated with the reason.
statements.explanation: A missing requirement is a decision that was never made, and recording it keeps the design history honest.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The code should be left as it is because the choice is already implemented.
statements.explanation: An unrecorded implicit decision stays hidden and may be wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A decision the agent made implicitly is hard to challenge because it was not written down.
statements.explanation: Unwritten decisions are not available for review.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The revised plan is a new version and needs its own review.
statements.explanation: A change to the plan is a new commitment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The episode shows that planning before acting is pointless because requirements change.
statements.explanation: A reviewed first plan is what makes visible which decision the new evidence reopens.

questions.stem: Midway through a task, an agent reports that fixing the bug properly requires editing a file outside the plan's declared scope. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The plan should be revised and the expansion approved before the edit.
statements.explanation: Scope is a boundary; widening it is a change of commitment that needs approval.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Describing the edit as an implementation detail of an in-scope step is an appropriate way to proceed.
statements.explanation: Relabeling an out-of-scope change hides it from review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Logging a warning while the edit proceeds is a sound design.
statements.explanation: A warning after the fact does not prevent the out-of-scope change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The scope field is advisory, so the agent may override it when it judges the change helpful.
statements.explanation: A scope field that the agent can override does not bound anything.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A request to leave the declared scope is a reason to halt or defer for a decision.
statements.explanation: It is a boundary crossing, which belongs among the halt or defer conditions.

questions.source: Formulation and the error of the third kind
questions.stem: A data team spends a quarter building a very accurate model that predicts which customers will open a marketing email. The business actually needed to know which customers are about to cancel their subscriptions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Raising the model's accuracy further would remove the problem.
statements.explanation: Accuracy on the wrong target is irrelevant to the need.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is an error of the third kind: a right answer to the wrong problem.
statements.explanation: The error lies in the formulation of the problem, not in the solution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Checking the finished result against the framing it already assumes is a weak test of whether the framing was right.
statements.explanation: An audit sharing the framing's assumptions cannot reveal that the framing is off.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is a Type II error, a false negative.
statements.explanation: A Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis within a given problem.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This is a Type I error, rejecting a true null hypothesis.
statements.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive inside a given test, not a wrong choice of problem.

questions.stem: A developer asks an LLM to frame a problem before writing down any framing of their own. Design researchers call an early, often unstated idea of what a problem is really about a primary generator. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Writing candidate framings first keeps a basis for judging the model's framing independently.
statements.explanation: Having one's own candidates gives something to compare against.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming a framing explicitly makes it available for challenge.
statements.explanation: An unstated framing cannot be questioned.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A primary generator shapes which solutions look natural to the designer.
statements.explanation: Whatever the first framing is, it narrows the solutions that are visible.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The model's framing can become the developer's anchor by default.
statements.explanation: The first framing named tends to set the reference point.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A developer can avoid having a primary generator by staying neutral.
statements.explanation: Some first idea of the problem forms regardless; the choice is whether to name it.

questions.stem: A team has written several candidate formulations of a problem and is writing the criteria for choosing among them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the criteria concern cost, time and feasibility alone, the process tends to pick the most tractable formulation.
statements.explanation: Feasibility-only scoring rewards what is easy to build or measure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The criteria are set before a candidate is scored.
statements.explanation: Criteria chosen after the scores can be bent toward a preferred option.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A salience criterion asks whether solving the problem addresses what matters in this context.
statements.explanation: Salience brings importance into the comparison.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model can propose candidate criteria while the team owns the final ones.
statements.explanation: Drafting can be delegated; the criteria encode what the team values.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Criteria written after the scores are known are better because they reflect what was learned.
statements.explanation: Criteria written afterward let the outcome shape the standard meant to judge it.

questions.stem: An engineer writes preconditions, postconditions and invariants for a function and then asks a coding agent to write the implementation. Tests are derived from the written contract, not from the agent's code. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tests derived from the contract stay independent of the agent's assumptions.
statements.explanation: The contract is an external reference.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent's statement that the contract holds is evidence that it holds.
statements.explanation: A claim of compliance is not evidence; the tests are.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Writing the contract first fixes boundary decisions while they are cheap to change.
statements.explanation: The decisions precede the code.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A precondition is what is required to hold before the function runs, and a postcondition is what holds afterward.
statements.explanation: Pre- and postconditions bracket the call.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tests derived from the agent's own implementation are as independent as tests derived from the contract.
statements.explanation: Tests built from the implementation encode its mistakes.

questions.stem: In a plan, the step "verify" declares that it comes after the step "build". The steps are drawn as a directed graph. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: build is a prerequisite of verify.
statements.explanation: A prerequisite is a step that must be done first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The edge in the graph runs from build to verify.
statements.explanation: Edges point from a prerequisite to the step that depends on it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: verify may start before build finishes if that is faster.
statements.explanation: The declared dependency forbids starting verify first.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The edge from build to verify is the place to attach an evidence condition for the handoff.
statements.explanation: Evidence belongs on the edges where work passes between steps.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A dependency is a directed obligation: verify requiring build does not mean build requires verify.
statements.explanation: The relation has a direction.

questions.stem: A build plan has four steps. Lint and test have no prerequisites. Build requires both lint and test. Deploy requires build. Check each statement that is a valid topological order of the steps.

statements.label: A
statements.text: build, lint, test, deploy
statements.explanation: Build would run before the lint and test steps it requires.

statements.label: B
statements.text: deploy, build, lint, test
statements.explanation: The order is reversed, so every step precedes its prerequisites.

statements.label: C
statements.text: lint, build, test, deploy
statements.explanation: Build would run before test, one of its prerequisites.

statements.label: D
statements.text: test, lint, deploy, build
statements.explanation: Deploy would run before build, its prerequisite.

statements.label: E
statements.text: lint, test, build, deploy
statements.explanation: Each step appears after all of its prerequisites.

questions.stem: In a plan graph, the steps migrate_schema and seed_test_data declare no dependency on each other, so they become ready in the same batch. Both write to the same database. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Being ready in the same batch means no declared dependency links the two steps.
statements.explanation: A batch collects steps whose declared prerequisites are done.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding an edge between the two steps would put them in sequence.
statements.explanation: A declared dependency orders the steps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ordering function detects shared writes by examining the steps.
statements.explanation: Ordering uses declared prerequisites only.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The absence of a declared dependency proves that the two steps can run at the same time safely.
statements.explanation: A shared resource can make them conflict.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A shared database is a hidden dependency that the graph does not represent.
statements.explanation: The graph encodes only what was declared.

questions.source: Duplicate id, unknown prerequisite and cycle
questions.stem: A function orders plan steps by their declared prerequisites and raises ValueError in three situations. Input 1 has two steps that both have the id "test". Input 2 is the single step {"id": "verify", "after": ["test"]} and no step named "test". Input 3 is {"id": "a", "after": ["b"]} and {"id": "b", "after": ["a"]}. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Input 2 is a dependency cycle.
statements.explanation: A cycle needs steps that depend on each other, directly or through a chain.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Input 1 is a duplicate-id error.
statements.explanation: Two steps share one identifier, so a prerequisite reference is ambiguous.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Input 3 is a dependency cycle, so no step can become ready first.
statements.explanation: Each step waits for the other.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Input 2 is an unknown-prerequisite error.
statements.explanation: The reference points to a step that does not exist.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sorting the ids alphabetically would resolve Input 3.
statements.explanation: A cycle is a property of the dependencies, not of the id order.

questions.stem: A plan declares three steps with no prerequisites: analyze, load and archive. In the real world, analyze needs the file that load produces. A function orders the steps by sorted id within each batch of ready steps and returns analyze, archive, load without error. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reviewer comparing each step's description with the declared prerequisites can find the omission.
statements.explanation: Finding a missing dependency needs a semantic comparison.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The ordering succeeds because the graph has no cycle.
statements.explanation: An acyclic graph can always be ordered.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The plan omits a real dependency of analyze on load, and the graph encodes the declared prerequisites alone.
statements.explanation: A missing edge is a defect the ordering cannot see.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The successful ordering shows the plan is correct.
statements.explanation: Acyclic does not mean executable; the order may violate a real dependency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A cycle check would detect the omitted dependency.
statements.explanation: A cycle check finds loops, not absent edges.

questions.stem: A team writes handoff conditions for a pipeline. A condition is testable when someone who did not build the pipeline can read it, observe the system and decide whether it holds. Check each condition that is testable in that sense.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Each claim in the draft is paired with the name of the source document it came from.
statements.explanation: A stranger can open the source and check the pairing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each figure in the draft appears in the supplied source table with the same value.
statements.explanation: It names an observable comparison with a defined outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The draft looks reasonable.
statements.explanation: Different reviewers would apply this differently.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The exit status of the test command is 0.
statements.explanation: A stranger can run the command and read the status.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The diff touches no file outside the scoped directory.
statements.explanation: A stranger can list the changed files and compare them with the directory.

questions.stem: A coding agent finishes a task and writes, "I ran the tests and they pass." A team is deciding what counts as evidence for moving the work to review. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A description of the tests as passing is as strong as a recorded exit status.
statements.explanation: A recorded exit status is an observation; a description is a report of one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test failure can be waved through if the agent explains why it does not matter.
statements.explanation: An explanation does not satisfy the handoff condition.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The sentence is evidence because the agent states it confidently.
statements.explanation: Confident wording is not an observation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The agent's summary of the output replaces the command output.
statements.explanation: A summary is the agent's description and can differ from what was produced.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sentence is a claim, not evidence.
statements.explanation: A claim reports what the agent says happened; evidence is something a reviewer can inspect.

questions.stem: A plan defines a handoff from a test-run step to a review step. The condition is that the targeted test passes, and the recorded test run shows a failure. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The work proceeds to review and the failure is noted there.
statements.explanation: A failed condition blocks the transition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A failure route is the planned next transition when an edge condition fails.
statements.explanation: Examples are repair, halt or defer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent's assertion that the test passes can satisfy the condition in place of the record.
statements.explanation: The condition refers to the recorded run, not to an assertion.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The handoff condition is not met.
statements.explanation: The evidence condition for the edge is unsatisfied.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The failing test shows that the plan graph contains a cycle.
statements.explanation: A test failure concerns the work, not the dependency structure.

questions.stem: Handoff conditions differ in who can apply them. Condition 1 is "the exit status of the test command is 0". Condition 2 is "the cited regulatory clause actually governs the proposed change". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Condition 2 needs a qualified person to judge it.
statements.explanation: Whether a clause governs a change is an interpretation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming who applies each condition is part of making the handoff testable.
statements.explanation: A condition with no applicant is not applied.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Condition 2 should be dropped from the plan because it needs human judgment.
statements.explanation: Human judgment is a legitimate evidence condition when an accountable owner is named.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Condition 2 is as mechanical as Condition 1 once the clause is cited.
statements.explanation: Citing a clause does not decide whether it governs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Condition 1 can be applied by a machine.
statements.explanation: It is a mechanical check of a value.

questions.stem: A reviewer ends a plan review with a written sign-off whose lines state what was checked, how it was checked, what was not checked, what is not claimed, and whether the reviewer signs or withholds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fluent sign-off drafted by a model is as good as one written from the reviewer's own record.
statements.explanation: A sign-off is only worth what the reviewer's record supports.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The line on what was not checked shows the limits of the sign-off.
statements.explanation: Stating the gaps keeps the sign-off from overclaiming.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sign-off on a plan claims less than a sign-off on a result: the plan survived the described review, not that the work succeeded.
statements.explanation: A plan review concerns the proposal, not the outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Withholding a signature is an honest outcome when the evidence does not support signing.
statements.explanation: A sign-off that cannot be given should not be given.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sign-off states what is not claimed, which keeps it within the review that was done.
statements.explanation: Stated non-claims prevent the signature from being read as a broader assurance.

questions.stem: A reviewer, before approving a plan, imagines for each important field a plan that satisfies the field's wording but fails its purpose, and also asks an AI assistant for counterexamples to the plan. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A counterexample that slips through shows the field's entry needs tightening.
statements.explanation: The entry should be reworded so that the counterexample fails.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An assistant can generate candidate counterexamples, but the reviewer judges whether each one is real.
statements.explanation: Generating and judging are separate steps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the assistant finds no counterexample, the plan is shown to be sound.
statements.explanation: Finding none shows only that none was found.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A plan that meets the wording but fails the purpose is a counterexample to that wording.
statements.explanation: A counterexample shows the field is too loosely worded.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Counterexample review replaces the structural presence check.
statements.explanation: They test different things and both have a place.

questions.source: Spotting imprecise wording in a prompt
questions.stem: A developer tells Claude Code: "Quickly fix the login bug, touch whatever you need, and tell me when it is done." Check each statement that correctly identifies a problem with the wording.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The prompt asks for a plan to be reviewed before editing.
statements.explanation: The prompt asks for the fix directly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "tell me when it is done" gives no observable stop condition.
statements.explanation: Done is defined by the agent's judgment rather than by an observation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "fix the login bug" supplies a verification command.
statements.explanation: It names a goal and no observation that would confirm it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Quickly" specifies a turn budget.
statements.explanation: A budget is a stated limit, not a vague adverb.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "touch whatever you need" leaves the scope undefined.
statements.explanation: A scope names what may change and what stays untouched.

questions.source: Best prompt to plan before acting
questions.stem: A developer wants Claude Code to plan before acting on a refactor. Check each prompt that uses exact terms for that purpose.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Write a plan that sounds confident and mark it approved so we can save time."
statements.explanation: Approval is an act by a person, not text.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Plan carefully in your head and show me the finished work."
statements.explanation: A private plan cannot be reviewed before action.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Propose a plan with objective, scope, steps, tools, risks, verification and stop. Do not modify files until I approve."
statements.explanation: It names the fields and the approval gate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Think hard about it, make a good plan and then go ahead and do it."
statements.explanation: This lets the agent proceed without review.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Make a plan with as many steps as possible so it is thorough."
statements.explanation: Step count is not a field of the plan and does not make it reviewable.

questions.source: Plan mode, permission and approval gate
questions.stem: In Claude Code, plan mode has the model read and analyze the project and present a plan for the user to approve before it edits files. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The plan presented is a proposal until the user approves it.
statements.explanation: Approval is a separate act.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Permission to run a tool is the same thing as approval of the plan.
statements.explanation: Permitting a tool call does not approve the plan.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tool permission prompt asks whether one action may run, while an approval gate asks whether a reviewed plan or result may advance.
statements.explanation: They check different things at different levels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Plan mode is the same as a mode that accepts edits automatically.
statements.explanation: Plan mode withholds edits until approval.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The user's approval of the plan is an approval gate.
statements.explanation: A gate is a point where work waits for a person's decision.

questions.stem: A plan's risks field reads "data loss; wrong output; cost overrun", with no mitigation, owner or trigger given for any item. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A risk is stronger when it is tied to a mitigation, an owner or a stop trigger.
statements.explanation: The tie makes the entry something a reviewer can challenge.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The risks field is adequate when it is short.
statements.explanation: Length says nothing about whether the entries can be challenged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A risk with a trigger can be turned into a halt condition in the stop field.
statements.explanation: The trigger links risks to the exits.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A risks entry names how the plan could fail, while the verification entry names how success is observed.
statements.explanation: The two fields answer different questions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A bare list of risk names fills the field without being concretely challengeable.
statements.explanation: A reviewer cannot dispute "data loss" without a stated cause or response.

questions.source: What to delegate and what to own
questions.stem: A developer decides which parts of a plan to hand to an AI assistant for a first draft that the developer then reviews, and which parts to answer personally. Check each statement that describes a part reasonable to hand over for a first draft.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Making the final selection among the formulations.
statements.explanation: The selection encodes what the team values and the team answers for it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Writing several candidate formulations of the problem.
statements.explanation: Generating candidates is drafting work that a person then compares.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Signing off on the plan.
statements.explanation: A sign-off is an act of an accountable person.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Deciding whether the plan is approved for execution.
statements.explanation: Approval is a decision by a person, not a draft.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Proposing candidate criteria for choosing among the formulations.
statements.explanation: Criteria can be drafted by a model and owned by the team.

questions.stem: A plan's steps include "read the customer table and compute churn rates". The customer table contains personal data. The inputs field lists only the source files of the analysis code, and the scope field excludes personal data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reordering the steps resolves the contradiction.
statements.explanation: The contradiction is between the fields, not in the order.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The data that the steps read is missing from the inputs field.
statements.explanation: The inputs field should name what the work starts from.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The steps contradict the scope, because reading the table touches excluded data.
statements.explanation: A cross-field review compares fields with one another.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A presence check on the eight fields would flag the problem.
statements.explanation: Each field is present and nonempty.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An inputs field that lists filenames is adequate without provenance or version.
statements.explanation: Provenance and version tell a reviewer what exactly the work depends on.

questions.stem: A developer gives Claude a tool definition for a function `convert_currency`: a name, a description, and an input schema listing `from`, `to` and `amount`. Claude replies with a structured block naming `convert_currency` with three arguments. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The input schema is code that checks the arguments at run time.
statements.explanation: The input schema is a description that guides how Claude forms arguments; checking is application code.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The tool definition is the code that performs the currency conversion.
statements.explanation: The definition is only a description (name, description, input schema); the implementation lives in application code.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The structured reply is a tool call (a tool_use block): a proposal expressed as data that the application decides how to handle.
statements.explanation: A tool_use block is a request, and the application, not the model, runs or refuses it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The model executes the function itself once the definition is supplied.
statements.explanation: Execution happens in the application's own runtime, outside the model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Declaring `amount` as a number in the schema guarantees the arguments arrive as a number, so validation in the application is redundant.
statements.explanation: The schema guides generation but does not enforce anything; the application still validates arguments.

questions.stem: Match the term to the behaviour. In a Claude API tool-using exchange, which statements pair a term with the correct meaning? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The tool_use_id on a tool_result matches the identifier of the tool_use it answers.
statements.explanation: Correspondence by identifier is how requests and results are paired.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tool_result block is produced by the model to announce which tool it wants.
statements.explanation: A tool_result carries the output back to the model; the model announces its request with tool_use.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The tool_use_id is a checksum that proves the result content is correct.
statements.explanation: The identifier only ties a result to its request; it says nothing about correctness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tool_result is returned to the model in an assistant-role message.
statements.explanation: Results travel back as the user side of the conversation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tool_use block is the model's request to run a named tool with arguments.
statements.explanation: tool_use is the request block that appears in an assistant message.

questions.stem: A controller reads the stop_reason field of each response from the Claude Messages API. Which statements about stop reasons are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: `max_tokens` signals that the output hit its limit, so a tool call in that response may have incomplete arguments.
statements.explanation: A truncated response can end mid-structure and needs an explicit policy, not execution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: `tool_use` signals that the application should run the requested tools and send results back.
statements.explanation: The controller must act on the request to continue the loop.

statements.label: C
statements.text: `tool_use` signals that the response was cut off at the output limit.
statements.explanation: tool_use means the model is waiting for the application to run requested tools; truncation is max_tokens.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A max_tokens stop is a truncation, which is a different exit from successful completion.
statements.explanation: Truncation and other stops are not completion; the exit should be named for what happened.

statements.label: E
statements.text: `end_turn` signals that the model finished its turn naturally and is not waiting on a tool.
statements.explanation: end_turn is the normal completion signal.

questions.stem: A team describes two designs. In design one, a person sets a fixed sequence: extract fields, validate, summarise, each step in code. In design two, the model chooses which tool to call next, sees the result, and decides whether to call another until it decides it is done. Which statements name these correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Design one is an agent loop because it calls the model.
statements.explanation: Calling a model inside a fixed sequence is still a workflow.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using tools does not by itself make a design an agent loop; what matters is who directs the control flow.
statements.explanation: Both designs call tools or models, and only design two lets the model choose the path.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Design two is an agent loop: the model directs the control flow across repeated tool calls.
statements.explanation: In an agent loop the model picks the next action based on tool results.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A turn limit (iteration cap) bounds the number of model requests in design two and so bounds its cost.
statements.explanation: A cap prevents unbounded continuation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Design one is a workflow: the control flow is fixed in advance by code.
statements.explanation: In a workflow the path through the steps is predetermined.

questions.stem: A dispatcher is the code that maps a tool name from a tool call to an operation. Which statements describe good dispatcher design? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A try/except around the lookup makes an open namespace lookup safe.
statements.explanation: Error handling afterwards does not restrict which functions can be reached.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An allowlist restricts the dispatcher to a closed set of named operations.
statements.explanation: An allowlist separates what is permitted from whatever name the model emits.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Argument rules are a separate layer from the allowlist, because a permitted tool can still receive harmful arguments.
statements.explanation: An allowed operation with bad arguments can still do damage.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Looking up the model's requested name in the program's global namespace is safe because the model is shown a list of advertised tools.
statements.explanation: A model can emit a name that was never advertised, by mistake or because untrusted text steered it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The model, not the application, decides what a requested tool name means.
statements.explanation: Mapping a name to behaviour is application logic.

questions.stem: A tool `write_file(path, content)` is meant to write inside a workspace directory. The model proposes a path that begins with the workspace prefix and then climbs out with `..` segments. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A check that the path string begins with the workspace prefix would reject it.
statements.explanation: The prefix is present, so a plain string-prefix check accepts the path.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Resolving the path to its canonical form before comparing it with the root exposes the escape.
statements.explanation: A canonical path has `..` and links resolved to the real location.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tool description steers the model but does not constrain the code that performs the write.
statements.explanation: Enforcement belongs in the application, for example in a resolved-path check.

statements.label: D
