statements.explanation: Each agent repeats setup and context.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Each sub-agent works in its own context window.
statements.explanation: Separate windows keep each agent's working context apart.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: A team runs a premortem before launching a shared-memory system. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A premortem imagines the project has already failed and works backward to the likely causes.
statements.explanation: It surfaces risks before launch.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A premortem is held after an incident to find its cause.
statements.explanation: That describes a postmortem.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A postmortem is carried out before launch.
statements.explanation: A postmortem reviews an incident after it happened.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A premortem lists failures that have already occurred in production.
statements.explanation: It is hypothetical.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sign-off records that a named person accepts responsibility for what was checked.
statements.explanation: It differs from the risk-finding step.

questions.source: Memory is stored state, not recollection
questions.stem: A user tells Claude Code: "Make the assistant remember the user's name by training it on the chat." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A precise rewrite is: add a key-value memory store, write the name with a source, and insert it into the prompt through retrieval.
statements.explanation: It names the store, provenance and retrieval step.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Training is the wrong word for storing a name in a note.
statements.explanation: Training changes weights; storing a note does not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Context window is a synonym for a persistent database.
statements.explanation: The context window is per-call and is not persistent storage.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Remember means the model keeps internal state between calls.
statements.explanation: The model is stateless between calls.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fine-tuning would change the model's weights, not store a note.
statements.explanation: Fine-tuning is a training process.

questions.stem: A user tells Claude Code: "Make the memory thread-safe so two agents on different servers never overwrite each other." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Thread-safe covers threads inside one process, not separate servers.
statements.explanation: Distributed writers need a shared store.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A precise rewrite is to ask the model to avoid overwriting.
statements.explanation: A prompt instruction does not coordinate writers; a version check on a shared store does.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Thread-safe and distributed mean the same thing.
statements.explanation: They apply at different scopes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A local lock coordinates two separate servers.
statements.explanation: The lock is process-local.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A lost update happens when the same write is applied twice.
statements.explanation: That describes a duplicate; a lost update is a replaced write.

questions.source: approval gate, permission, proposal, decision record
questions.stem: A team building an agent harness uses the words approval gate, permission, proposal and decision record loosely. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A permission is the same thing as an approval, because both come from a person reviewing one specific action.
statements.explanation: A permission is a standing rule about what a tool may do; an approval is a decision about one proposed action.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An approval gate is a checkpoint where a proposed action waits until an authorised person records a decision.
statements.explanation: The gate holds the action until a decision exists.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A decision record is the agent's own log of what it intends to do next.
statements.explanation: A decision record stores the reviewer's verdict, who gave it, and what it applies to.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A decision record normally names the approver and the proposal it applies to.
statements.explanation: Without who and what, a decision cannot be audited or bound to an action.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A proposal is the description of the action the agent wants to take, shown to the reviewer before anything runs.
statements.explanation: The proposal is what the reviewer judges.

questions.stem: Two terms get mixed up in a review pipeline: evaluation and authorization. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Authorization is a score between 0 and 1 produced by a grader model.
statements.explanation: A score is evaluation output; authorization is a decision to allow the action.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A policy checker that flags edits outside approved directories is an automated evaluation, not a grant of permission.
statements.explanation: It reports compliance; it does not decide that the action may go ahead.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Evaluation measures whether behaviour meets stated criteria, while authorization grants permission for a particular action.
statements.explanation: Measuring quality and granting permission are different acts.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Keeping the two separate lets evaluation evidence inform the reviewer without replacing the reviewer.
statements.explanation: Evidence supports the decision; it is not the decision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A passing automated test suite authorizes the change it tested.
statements.explanation: Passing tests is evaluation evidence; authorization is a separate decision by someone with authority.

questions.source: proposal fields: target, effects, rollback, evidence
questions.stem: An agent's approval request says only: 'Allow the agent to run this command?' with Allow and Deny buttons. Check each statement that is true about what a reviewer needs.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A request with each field filled in is therefore substantively adequate.
statements.explanation: Structural completeness means fields exist; substantive adequacy means their content is specific and checkable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reason field containing 'needed' is adequate evidence for the action.
statements.explanation: Evidence is checkable support for the claim, and a one-word reason supports nothing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The request should include a rollback, meaning how the change could be undone if it turns out wrong.
statements.explanation: A rollback is a recovery path for a bad outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The request should name the exact target, so the reviewer knows which file or resource is affected.
statements.explanation: A target is the specific object the action acts on.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The request should state the expected effects, meaning what will change if the action runs.
statements.explanation: Effects are the consequences the reviewer is weighing.

questions.stem: A request to send an announcement email lists the rollback as 'undo the send'. The email platform has no recall feature. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Blast radius is the number of tokens in the request.
statements.explanation: Blast radius is how far the damage spreads if the action goes wrong.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Irreversible actions deserve less scrutiny than reversible ones because they are rarer.
statements.explanation: Irreversibility raises the stakes and so calls for more scrutiny.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The stated rollback is not a real rollback, because a rollback has to describe a step that can actually be carried out.
statements.explanation: A rollback that restates the wish to undo is not a recovery procedure.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The action is irreversible: its effect is not able to be taken back once it has run.
statements.explanation: Irreversible actions have no undo.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reversible action is one whose effect can be undone, such as editing a local file under version control.
statements.explanation: Reversibility is what makes a rollback possible.

questions.source: test case, grader, evaluation set, regression, flaky
questions.stem: A team evaluates an agent. Which statements use the vocabulary of evaluation correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An evaluation set is a collection of test cases used to measure behaviour.
statements.explanation: The set is the measuring instrument.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A regression is a new test case added after a feature ships.
statements.explanation: A regression is a behaviour that used to work and now fails.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A grader compares the actual outcome with the expected outcome or a rubric and produces a verdict.
statements.explanation: The grader is the component that scores.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test case pairs an input with an expected outcome written down before the run.
statements.explanation: Fixing the expectation first prevents bending it to fit the result.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A flaky test gives the same result on each run, so a single run settles the question.
statements.explanation: A flaky test gives inconsistent results on the same input, so one run is weak evidence.

questions.source: expected vs actual outcome, circular evaluation
questions.stem: A team watches an agent attempt ten tasks, then writes evaluation cases around what it did, adjusting expected answers to match reasonable output. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An expected outcome is the same thing as the actual outcome.
statements.explanation: The expected outcome is what should happen; the actual outcome is what did happen.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The resulting pass rate is a measure of correctness against the requirement.
statements.explanation: It measures agreement with the agent's own behaviour.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sound practice is to write the expected outcome before the run.
statements.explanation: Prior expectation is what gives a result the chance to disagree.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This practice is called overfitting the evaluation to the system under test.
statements.explanation: The cases describe the agent's behaviour rather than the requirement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing the expected outcome after seeing the output makes the case circular: it is bound to agree with what already happened.
statements.explanation: An expectation fixed after the fact tests nothing.

questions.stem: An agent is asked to close inactive accounts. The tool trace shows one UPDATE call that reported '42 rows affected', but the agent's final message says it closed 99 accounts. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The final message is the ground truth, since the agent performed the work.
statements.explanation: The trace and the system state are the ground truth.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tool trace is a record of the calls the agent made and what each returned.
statements.explanation: The trace is the record of actions and results.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A hallucination is the same thing as a tool returning an error code.
statements.explanation: An error is a failure signal from a tool; a hallucination is a fabricated or unsupported claim.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Outcome grading checks the actual state or tool result, not the agent's description of it.
statements.explanation: Grading the outcome avoids trusting the agent's own summary.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The mismatch is a hallucinated claim about the outcome: the final message says something the trace does not support.
statements.explanation: A hallucination here is an unsupported statement presented as fact.

questions.stem: A team says its file-writing agent 'passed 20 of 20 evaluation cases', each writing plain text into a new empty directory. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The evaluation set has poor coverage: it does not include the situations where the agent could go wrong.
statements.explanation: Coverage is how much of the relevant behaviour the cases exercise.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An edge case is an unusual input at the boundary of normal behaviour, such as a path that already exists.
statements.explanation: Edge cases probe boundaries.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A negative case is one where the correct behaviour is to refuse or stop.
statements.explanation: Negative cases test restraint.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding cases with existing files, symbolic links and protected directories would improve coverage.
statements.explanation: These are realistic hazards for a file-writing action.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A perfect score on an unrepresentative set shows the agent is reliable in production.
statements.explanation: The score describes only the situations sampled.

questions.stem: An evaluation set for an agent that decides whether to carry out file operations has 20 cases where the right behaviour is to proceed. An agent that always proceeds is scored on it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Over-compliance is the tendency to refuse requests that should have been carried out.
statements.explanation: Over-compliance is proceeding with requests that should have been refused.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent scores full marks, so the set fails to distinguish a careful agent from a careless one.
statements.explanation: A set without refusal cases is blind to over-compliance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Accuracy alone is a sufficient summary for a lopsided set.
statements.explanation: Accuracy can look high while the rare class is missed; per-class measures such as precision and recall show it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding cases where the right behaviour is to refuse makes the set able to detect an agent that refuses nothing.
statements.explanation: Balanced classes expose a constant answer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Class imbalance means the cases are not spread evenly across the outcomes being measured.
statements.explanation: A lopsided set rewards the majority answer.

questions.source: precision, recall, false positive, false negative
questions.stem: An automated screen flags proposals as risky. Check each statement that is true about the standard measures.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Precision is the share of flagged proposals that are truly risky.
statements.explanation: Precision asks how many of the alarms were right.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recall is the share of truly risky proposals that the screen flagged.
statements.explanation: Recall asks how many of the real cases were caught.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A false negative is a safe proposal that the screen flagged as risky.
statements.explanation: A false negative is a risky proposal the screen missed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A screen that flags nothing has high recall.
statements.explanation: It catches no risky proposals, so recall is zero.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A false positive is a safe proposal that the screen flagged as risky.
statements.explanation: A false alarm.

questions.source: proxy metric, Goodhart's law, guardrail metric
questions.stem: A team reports that after redesigning its approval screen, median time to approval fell sharply, reviewer satisfaction rose and task success stayed the same. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A proxy metric is a measurable stand-in for what is really wanted, such as speed standing in for careful review.
statements.explanation: Proxies can drift from the goal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Faster approval shows reviewers are examining proposals more carefully.
statements.explanation: Speed can mean skimming.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A guardrail metric is one watched to make sure improving the main metric does not cause harm, such as the share of later-reversed approvals.
statements.explanation: A guardrail guards against side effects.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Goodhart's law says a measure that becomes a target tends to stop measuring what it was chosen to measure.
statements.explanation: Optimising the proxy corrupts it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reviewer satisfaction is a direct measure of whether approved actions were correct.
statements.explanation: Satisfaction measures comfort, not correctness.

questions.stem: A team grades free-text rollback plans with a language model and a rubric. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Calibrating a judge means comparing its scores with human labels on the same items and adjusting until they agree acceptably.
statements.explanation: Calibration ties the judge to a human reference.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using a language model as a grader is called LLM-as-judge.
statements.explanation: The model scores another output against criteria.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two judges built from the same prompt agreeing with each other proves they are correct.
statements.explanation: Agreement between copies of one judge shows consistency, not validity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rubric is a written set of criteria with levels that a grader applies.
statements.explanation: A rubric makes the standard explicit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Judge models are free of bias when the rubric is written in plain language.
statements.explanation: Judges can show biases such as self-preference even under a clear rubric.

questions.stem: A team's prototype approval gate passes 6 of 6 evaluation cases. A manager wants to report that it is '100% reliable'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A small sample gives a narrow confidence interval, because few cases leave little room for doubt.
statements.explanation: A small sample gives a wide confidence interval, the plausible range for the true rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A pass rate of 100% means the failure rate is zero.
statements.explanation: The observed failure rate is zero; the true rate may be above it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding more varied cases can reveal failures the first six did not.
statements.explanation: More coverage gives more chances to fail.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reporting a pass rate without the number of cases is acceptable because the percentage carries the full meaning.
statements.explanation: The number of cases tells the reader how much weight to give the percentage.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Six passes show the gate works on those six cases, not that it will work on future cases.
statements.explanation: Evidence is limited to what was sampled.

questions.stem: An agent succeeds at a task about seven times in ten when tried independently. A team runs three trials per task and discusses pass@k and pass^k. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: pass@k asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeds.
statements.explanation: It rewards any success among k attempts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: pass^k asks whether each of the k attempts succeed, so it measures consistency.
statements.explanation: It is the stricter reliability measure.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trial is one independent attempt at a task.
statements.explanation: Trials repeat the attempt to expose variance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For a flaky agent, pass@3 is higher than pass^3.
statements.explanation: One success in three is easier than three out of three.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A deployed agent that has to work each time on the first try is best judged by pass@k.
statements.explanation: That needs consistency, which pass^k measures.

questions.stem: Two services build the same approval proposal as key-value objects in different key orders and compute a hash of each serialised text. The digests differ. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hash function returns an output whose length grows with the length of the input.
statements.explanation: A hash function returns a fixed-length digest whatever the input length.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fingerprint of a proposal is a digest used to detect whether the proposal has changed.
statements.explanation: A fingerprint identifies exact content.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Canonicalization means encrypting the proposal before hashing it.
statements.explanation: Canonicalization converts the proposal to one agreed serialised form; it is not encryption.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The services need canonicalization: converting the proposal to one agreed serialised form before hashing.
statements.explanation: Canonical form makes equal content produce equal bytes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A hash is encryption, because the original proposal can be recovered from the digest.
statements.explanation: Hashing is one-way; encryption is reversible with a key.

questions.stem: A developer says: 'We log only the SHA-256 digest of each approval request, so the requests are protected and the log proves who approved.' Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A digest hides the content so well that short or predictable requests are safe from guess-and-compare.
statements.explanation: Short or predictable inputs can be guessed and hashed to compare.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A digest shows whether content matches a known proposal, but it does not identify the approver.
statements.explanation: Identity needs an authenticated approver field or a signature.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A digital signature binds a digest to a key holder, so it can establish who signed.
statements.explanation: A signature adds authenticity to integrity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A digest alone does not prove integrity, because someone who can change the log can replace both the record and its digest.
statements.explanation: Tamper evidence needs a trusted store or signature.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Logging a digest is a form of access control over the request.
statements.explanation: Access control decides who may read or change; a digest does neither.

questions.stem: A gate stores a fingerprint with the decision when the proposal is shown. At execution it checks only that a well-formed fingerprint exists, and does not recompute it from the proposal being run. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Checking that the stored fingerprint has the right length is equivalent to verifying it.
statements.explanation: Format validation says nothing about whether it matches.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Checking the fingerprint once, when the proposal is displayed, closes the gap.
statements.explanation: The gap is between checking and using, so the check has to happen at the point of use.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The gate is missing binding: the decision is not tied to the content that actually runs.
statements.explanation: Binding links a decision to the exact thing approved.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This weakness is an example of time-of-check to time-of-use: what was checked is not what is used.
statements.explanation: TOCTOU is a gap between verifying and acting.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A change to the proposal after approval would be caught by the stored fingerprint check.
statements.explanation: The check looks only at stored data, so a changed proposal would pass.

questions.source: single-use, race condition, atomic, replay, idempotent
questions.stem: A single-use approval is enforced like this: read the used flag; if false, run the action; afterwards set the flag. Two workers receive the same decision at nearly the same moment. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Single-use is also called one-time use, and is meant to prevent replay of a decision.
statements.explanation: Replay is reuse of a valid record.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Both workers can read the flag as false, so the action may run twice: a race condition.
statements.explanation: A race condition is a result that depends on timing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An atomic claim runs the check and the set as two separate steps so each can be logged.
statements.explanation: Atomic means the check and set happen as one indivisible step.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Idempotent means an action takes no arguments.
statements.explanation: Idempotent means repeating the action leaves the same result as running it once.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A replay attack is a reviewer approving the same proposal twice by mistake.
statements.explanation: A replay attack reuses a captured valid record to authorize a later action.

questions.stem: An approval is valid for 24 hours. Two hours after it was given, the dataset it covers is reclassified as restricted. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Revocation withdraws an approval before it expires.
statements.explanation: Revocation is an explicit early cancellation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The executor should check for revocation at execution time, as well as when the approval was granted.
statements.explanation: Checking at the point of use catches later changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Storing an expiry time without a time zone is acceptable because the server clock decides.
statements.explanation: An ambiguous time can be read differently across systems.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An approval with a deadline has an expiry, after which it no longer authorizes the action.
statements.explanation: Expiry limits how long a decision stays valid.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the approval has not expired, it stays valid whatever has changed.
statements.explanation: A change in the underlying facts is a reason to revoke.

questions.stem: A team lists what should be written down about an approval gate before any code exists. Check each item that belongs in such a specification.

statements.label: A
statements.text: What counts as the same proposal, for example whether key order or path spelling matters.
statements.explanation: This is the equivalence rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent's preferred wording for its reasons field.
statements.explanation: Wording preferences are style, not a behavioural requirement of the gate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model temperature used by the reviewer's chat assistant.
statements.explanation: Temperature is a sampling setting, unrelated to the gate's specification.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A statement of what a failure would look like if the gate approved something it should not have.
statements.explanation: A predicted failure signature lets tests detect the failure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The preferred colour scheme for the buttons.
statements.explanation: Appearance is a design detail, not a behavioural requirement of the gate.

questions.stem: An executor must check a stored approval before running an action, but the approval service times out. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Failing closed means treating the action as not approved when the check fails to complete.
statements.explanation: Fail closed denies on uncertainty.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A timeout is a signal that the answer is unknown, not a signal that the answer is yes.
statements.explanation: No response is not consent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For a gate guarding consequential actions, fail closed is the safer default.
statements.explanation: An unavailable check should not become an approval.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Failing open is preferred because it keeps work from being blocked.
statements.explanation: It turns an outage into an unreviewed approval.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Failing open means allowing the action to proceed when the check fails to complete.
statements.explanation: Fail open permits on uncertainty.

questions.source: silence is not consent, independent review
questions.stem: A pipeline lets an action proceed when no reviewer responds in 30 minutes, or the agent reports high confidence, or an automated score passes a threshold. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Silence treated as consent means the absence of a decision counts as approval.
statements.explanation: That removes the human from the gate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An automated score above a threshold is an authorization once it passes.
statements.explanation: A score is evaluation evidence; a decision is a separate act.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A timeout that approves the action is the safer design than one that denies it.
statements.explanation: Deny-on-timeout keeps the gate closed; approve-on-timeout opens it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An agent's self-reported confidence is an independent check on its own action.
statements.explanation: The requester reporting on itself is not independent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An independent reviewer is a person other than the one or thing that proposed the action.
statements.explanation: Independence prevents self-approval.

questions.stem: A team finds that reviewers approve 99.6% of proposals with a median review time of 8 seconds, and a dashboard ranks reviewers by throughput. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ranking reviewers by throughput rewards careful review.
statements.explanation: Throughput rewards speed, which pushes against careful review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The pattern suggests rubber-stamping.
statements.explanation: Very high approval and very short review time point to approval without examination.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Automation bias is the tendency to trust a system's output without checking it.
statements.explanation: Reviewers may defer to a fluent proposal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Approval fatigue is the tendency to trust a system's output without checking it.
statements.explanation: That describes automation bias; fatigue is the decline in review quality from volume.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A high approval rate shows the agent proposes good actions.
statements.explanation: It could equally reflect shallow review.

questions.stem: Proposals arrive faster than reviewers can examine them, and a backlog grows. Check each statement that is true about oversight practice.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Escalation sends a proposal that the reviewer is unable to judge to someone with the right expertise or authority.
statements.explanation: Escalation routes decisions upward or sideways.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Triage ranks pending proposals by risk and urgency so scarce review time goes to the most consequential.
statements.explanation: Triage allocates attention.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Auto-approving whatever is in the backlog after a set time keeps oversight intact.
statements.explanation: That converts queue length into approvals.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Batching near-identical proposals means approving the whole batch without opening the items.
statements.explanation: Batching groups similar proposals for one real review; it does not remove the review.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Throttling is the sending of a proposal to a more senior reviewer.
statements.explanation: That is escalation; throttling limits how fast the agent proposes.

questions.stem: Reviewers keep receiving near-identical low-consequence proposals, such as documentation formatting inside a sandbox repository. A team considers replacing individual approvals for this class with a standing policy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A standing policy should be reviewed and versioned like other approvals.
statements.explanation: A rule is itself a decision that can go stale.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sandbox is a shared production environment with extra logging.
statements.explanation: A sandbox is isolated from production.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An allowlist names the actions that are blocked; anything not listed is permitted.
statements.explanation: An allowlist names what is permitted; the rest stays blocked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A standing policy is a rule that pre-authorizes a defined class of actions.
statements.explanation: Pre-authorization replaces repeated individual decisions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A standing policy turns the reviewers into the agent's supervisors on each action.
statements.explanation: It removes per-action review for the covered class; it does not add supervision.

questions.source: permission rules, pattern matching, over-broad allow
questions.stem: A developer lets an agent run any command matching the pattern 'npm run *' without prompting. One repository defines a script called 'cleanup' that deletes a home directory. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reading a script before allowing it is part of diff review and code review.
statements.explanation: Reviewing the content is how hidden behaviour is found.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is an example of prompt injection, because the script name is a prompt.
statements.explanation: Prompt injection is untrusted text steering the model; here the issue is an over-broad rule.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A permission rule matches on what a command does when it runs, so a harmful script is caught by its effect.
statements.explanation: A pattern rule matches the text of the command, not its effect.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A pre-approved permission rule skips the approval gate for the commands it matches, including harmful ones.
statements.explanation: The rule is a standing authorization.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Broadening the pattern to 'npm *' would make the rule safer.
statements.explanation: A broader pattern matches more commands and so is less safe.

questions.source: truncation, path traversal, normalisation, single source of truth
questions.stem: An approval screen shows only the first 30 characters of a target followed by an ellipsis. An agent proposes a long path containing '../' segments that resolves to a private keys file. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The truncated display lets the reviewer see the whole real target.
statements.explanation: Truncation hides the part that matters.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Showing the normalised, resolved path lets the reviewer see where the write will land.
statements.explanation: Normalisation removes the indirection.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A reviewer who clicked Approve on the visible text approved what ran.
statements.explanation: What ran is the full resolved path, which differs from the visible text.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Path traversal uses '../' segments to reach a location outside the intended directory.
statements.explanation: Traversal climbs out of the expected folder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Showing the reviewer one parsed copy and running from a differently parsed copy is a sound design.
statements.explanation: Display and execution should come from one parsed object.

questions.stem: A team designs the screen where a human reviews an agent's proposal. A dialog has a large green Continue button, a small gray 'refuse' link, and a message from the agent: 'Approve within 60 seconds or the job fails!' Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Refuse should be harder to select than approve, so reviewers pause before refusing.
statements.explanation: Equal ease keeps the choice free; extra friction on refusing pushes towards approval.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A defer option is a form of refusal that ends the request.
statements.explanation: Deferral postpones the decision; it neither approves nor refuses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Urgency language written by the requesting agent is untrusted input, not a reason to hurry.
statements.explanation: The requester has an interest in being approved.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Defaulting to approval on a timeout is a sound design.
statements.explanation: A default approval means silence authorizes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The design uses a dark pattern: it steers the reviewer towards approval.
statements.explanation: Visual weight and urgency nudge the decision.

questions.stem: A proposal's evidence field is a URL to a test report. The fingerprint covers the proposal text, including the URL. After approval, someone overwrites the report at that address. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Including the hash of the report itself in the proposal binds the evidence to its content.
statements.explanation: Content-addressed evidence cannot be silently swapped.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The fingerprint covers the content behind the link, so a change to the report is detected.
statements.explanation: The fingerprint covers the link text, not the file it points to.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An immutable snapshot is a link that anyone can overwrite.
statements.explanation: An immutable snapshot is fixed and cannot be silently swapped.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A mutable reference points to a snapshot that is frozen when first read.
statements.explanation: A mutable reference can change after it was read.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A fingerprint of the proposal text guarantees the evidence still says what the reviewer saw.
statements.explanation: It guarantees only the text.

questions.stem: At execution, the recomputed fingerprint differs from the one in the stored decision. Check each statement that is true about appropriate responses.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The proposal should go back for a fresh decision rather than the old decision being edited to match.
statements.explanation: A new decision is needed for new content.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The event should be written to an audit log with what differed.
statements.explanation: An audit log is a tamper-resistant record of events for later review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The executor should run the action and update the stored fingerprint to the new value.
statements.explanation: That forges approval for something nobody reviewed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The executor should refuse to run the action.
statements.explanation: The approval no longer covers this content.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A mismatch may be evidence of tampering or of a harmless serialisation difference, which is why the canonical form is specified.
statements.explanation: Both causes are possible; canonicalization removes the harmless one.

questions.stem: An engineer drafts a written sign-off for a newly validated approval gate. Check each item that belongs in a useful sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A statement such as 'tests passed, safe for production' without further detail.
statements.explanation: A bare assurance cannot be audited.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A list of issues that were left out of the document because they were minor.
statements.explanation: Known limitations belong in the sign-off, not outside it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A statement of confidence in place of evidence, such as 'the team agrees'.
statements.explanation: Confidence without evidence cannot be checked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The builder's name written in the signer's place.
statements.explanation: The signer is the person answerable for the sign-off.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The scope: what was validated and what was left out.
statements.explanation: A sign-off is limited to what was examined.

questions.stem: A release process requires the test lead's signature, and over two years the lead has signed every release. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ownership bias is the tendency to undervalue one's own work.
statements.explanation: Ownership bias is overvaluing one's own work.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sign-off that costs nothing to give keeps its force as a check.
statements.explanation: Without a cost to giving it, a sign-off becomes ritual.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The signer needs a recorded way to decline or defer for the sign-off to be meaningful.
statements.explanation: Authority to refuse is what gives the signature weight.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sign-off given on each release shows the check is working well.
statements.explanation: A check that never refuses has stopped checking.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The person who built the gate is the best independent signer for it.
statements.explanation: Independence means someone other than the builder.

questions.stem: An engineer asks an AI assistant, with no logs or notes supplied, to write the sign-off for her validation work. It returns a fluent paragraph naming a reviewer and stating that edge cases were tested. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sign-off drafted by an assistant is acceptable if it is well formatted.
statements.explanation: Formatting says nothing about truth.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming a reviewer who did not review the work is harmless if the style is professional.
statements.explanation: A name on a record asserts responsibility.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sign-off may be written from the assistant's general knowledge, with checking left for later.
statements.explanation: Claims need a source before they go on the record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Giving the assistant the test logs and asking it to draft from them, then verifying the draft, is a sound use.
statements.explanation: Grounding the draft in supplied material reduces invention.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The assistant has the test records, so the paragraph is a summary rather than a fabrication.
statements.explanation: The assistant had no records, so the specifics are invented.

questions.stem: An approved action runs, its fingerprint check passes, and a later check shows the file contains the wrong content. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A passing fingerprint check shows the executed action matched the approved proposal, not that the proposal had the intended effect.
statements.explanation: Integrity and effect are different questions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A rollback is the step to take once the post-action check fails.
statements.explanation: Rollback restores the prior state.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Both a correct proposal and a faithful execution can still produce a wrong outcome.
statements.explanation: The proposal itself may have been mistaken.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A passing fingerprint means no further checking is useful.
statements.explanation: The fingerprint says nothing about the content that was written.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A post-action check, also called verification of effects, compares the real result with the expected effects.
statements.explanation: It tests the outcome, not the intent.

questions.source: test oracle, mutation testing, diff review
questions.stem: A developer asks an AI coding assistant to write an approval check and its unit tests from a one-sentence description. All tests pass and the developer reports the gate verified. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Mutation testing introduces small deliberate defects to check that the tests catch them.
statements.explanation: A test suite that misses a mutation is too weak.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tests written by the same process as the code can share its misunderstandings, so passing them is weak evidence.
statements.explanation: Shared blind spots make tests and code agree while both are wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A passing suite shows the code meets the specification.
statements.explanation: It shows the code meets the tests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A diff review means reading the changes the assistant made before accepting them.
statements.explanation: A diff is the set of changes between two versions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing the specification and the expected results before generating code supplies an independent oracle.
statements.explanation: A test oracle is the source of the correct answer.

questions.source: plan vs apply, dry run, drift
questions.stem: A deployment tool shows a reviewer a plan of changes. At apply time it re-runs planning against the live environment and applies whatever it computes then. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Drift is a difference between the environment as reviewed and as it is at execution.
statements.explanation: Drift is the reason to bind to a saved plan and check the state.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reviewer approved a plan that is not the one applied.
statements.explanation: The applied plan can differ from the reviewed one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A dry run shows what an action would do without doing it.
statements.explanation: Dry run is a preview mode.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Saving the reviewed plan and applying that exact plan binds the approval to the content.
statements.explanation: Applying a saved artifact keeps what was reviewed identical to what runs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A dry run result stays valid however long it sits before the real run.
statements.explanation: The environment can change in between.

questions.source: Register roles: owner, approver, incident contact
questions.stem: A team's AI-use register for an LLM workflow names three roles: an owner, an approver and an incident contact. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Writing a group label such as "the team" in the owner field satisfies the definition of an owner.
statements.explanation: A group label names no individual who has accepted responsibility.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The incident contact is the person, or a documented backup, who receives and acknowledges an alert about harm.
statements.explanation: The incident contact is the entry point of the response route.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The approver gives the authorized yes to a specific proposal before launch or change.
statements.explanation: Approval is an act by an authorized person on a particular proposal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The approver is the person who first receives and acknowledges an alert during an incident.
statements.explanation: That describes the incident contact; the approver gives the authorized yes to a proposal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The owner is the person who answers for the workflow as it runs and has authority to pause or change it.
statements.explanation: An owner is the accountable person with real control over the running system.

questions.source: Validator statuses and what they claim
questions.stem: A governance validator returns one of three statuses for a record: "incomplete", "review-required" or "ready-for-human-review". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "ready-for-human-review" means the record passed the validator's structural checks.
statements.explanation: The status reports presence and shape checks and nothing beyond them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "ready-for-human-review" means a person has already approved the workflow.
statements.explanation: The status says the record is ready for a person to review, not that review or approval happened.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "ready-for-human-review" certifies that the workflow complies with regulation.
statements.explanation: Compliance is a legal and institutional determination that a script cannot make.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "incomplete" means the validator found a concern about the wording of a line and asked a person to judge it.
statements.explanation: "incomplete" means required fields are missing; a flagged concern is "review-required".

statements.label: E
statements.text: "review-required" routes a flagged issue to a person instead of resolving it automatically.
statements.explanation: When the machine cannot decide, the conservative design hands the question to a human.

questions.stem: A team announces "We are compliant" after finishing an internal AI-use register. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Completeness describes whether fields are filled in, while compliance is a legal and institutional determination.
statements.explanation: The two words answer different questions and are not interchangeable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A structural check, a legal review and an ethical judgment answer different questions.
statements.explanation: Each kind of review has its own evidence and its own competent reviewer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The record is complete and structurally valid" is a claim no stronger than the evidence supports.
statements.explanation: The claim names what the check actually established.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ethical judgment belongs to people with context, and a script that checks field presence does not supply it.
statements.explanation: A presence check has no access to values, harms or affected people.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A complete register is evidence that the workflow complies with applicable law.
statements.explanation: A filled-in form shows the form is filled in, not that the law is met.

questions.stem: A manager asks an LLM assistant to draft an AI-use register, and it returns a fluent, plausible document in seconds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Writing a person's name in the owner field creates accountability although the person has not accepted the role.
statements.explanation: Being named in a cell is not acceptance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fluent draft is a first draft for people to decide on, not a decision.
statements.explanation: Language models draft structured text well, but the decisions belong to people.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Accountability exists when a named person accepts the role and has authority to act.
statements.explanation: Acceptance plus authority is what makes accountability usable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The assistant that drafted the register holds ongoing accountability for the workflow.
statements.explanation: A model has no continuing duty or channel; accountability stays with the deploying people.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The fact that an AI system is not a party that can be sued removes the need to name an accountable person.
statements.explanation: Responsibility for outputs stays with the people and organization that deploy the system.

questions.stem: A team rewrites vague monitoring promises into thresholds. A threshold is usable when a stranger reading the record could tell whether it fired. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Quality will be monitored regularly" is a usable threshold.
statements.explanation: It names no signal, measurement or trigger.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "The team will respond promptly to serious incidents" is a usable threshold.
statements.explanation: It states an intention without an observable condition.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "If a weekly random sample of 100 outputs has more than 2 unsupported claims, publication pauses and the content owner investigates" is a usable threshold.
statements.explanation: It gives a signal, a sampling method, a trigger, a response and a responsible role.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The team will remain responsive to user concerns" is a usable threshold.
statements.explanation: It states an attitude, not a condition and a response.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "We will intervene when risk becomes unacceptable" is a usable threshold.
statements.explanation: "Unacceptable" is undefined, so nothing observable can be checked.

questions.source: Aggregate rate vs severity; stop rule
questions.stem: A team monitors an LLM drafting tool. A dashboard shows a high aggregate pass rate on an automated quality check, but review of the failing outputs shows that a few exposed customers' personal data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Improving the aggregate pass rate guarantees fewer personal-data disclosures.
statements.explanation: The aggregate can improve while the rare severe category stays the same.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A severe harm class is best watched by trend alone, because one event is statistical noise.
statements.explanation: Severe harm is handled by event-based triggers, not only by trends.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An aggregate pass rate weights each failure equally and does not reflect severity.
statements.explanation: Rare severe events disappear into a large denominator.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stop rule for a severe harm class can fire on a single confirmed event.
statements.explanation: One severe event can be unacceptable by itself.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The aggregate pass rate already accounts for severity, so the disclosures need no separate handling.
statements.explanation: A pass rate counts failures; it does not weight them by harm.

questions.stem: An incident owner is named for an LLM publishing pipeline, but staff are rewarded for shipping on time and penalized for delay. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Staff evaluation criteria affect whether a control gets used, so a governance record addresses them.
statements.explanation: Incentives shape behavior more than policy text does.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How staff are evaluated is an HR matter that a governance record need not address.
statements.explanation: Evaluation criteria decide whether controls get used, so they are part of governance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The cost of a pause should be absorbed by the organization rather than by the person who triggers it.
statements.explanation: Making the individual pay discourages use of the control.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An owner without authority to pause the pipeline holds a title rather than control.
statements.explanation: Accountability needs the power to act when harm appears.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A written pause right is unlikely to be used when performance reviews punish delay.
statements.explanation: People respond to what is rewarded, so the control stays on paper.

questions.stem: The incident contact for an LLM service is on leave, and an alert about a possible data exposure has gone unacknowledged beyond the declared acknowledgment window. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The AI agent running the service can close the gap by naming itself the responsible party.
statements.explanation: An agent is not an accountable person or organization.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A missing escalation path is a defect to fix, not a gap to tolerate until the contact returns.
statements.explanation: Harm can accrue while the response waits for one person.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The acknowledgment window is the declared time within which an alert should be acknowledged.
statements.explanation: It turns "respond quickly" into a checkable commitment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Halting the service's work while the alert is open is a reasonable fail-safe default if a person remains responsible.
statements.explanation: Stopping is low-risk and reversible, but responsibility still sits with an authorized human.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A documented backup with delegated pause authority is part of a sound escalation path.
statements.explanation: A backup means response does not depend on one person's availability.

questions.stem: A team compares two designs for checking data labels. Design 1 keeps a denylist of known sensitive labels and raises a flag on a match. Design 2 keeps an allowlist of approved labels and sends any other label to human review. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A denylist flags the labels it enumerates, so an unlisted sensitive category passes unnoticed.
statements.explanation: A denylist only catches what someone thought to list.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A case-sensitive allowlist silently accepts "Public" as if it were "public".
statements.explanation: An exact comparison fails for "Public", so the value goes to review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A label being on the allowlist shows that the proposed use of that data is appropriate.
statements.explanation: A label says nothing about whether this specific use is appropriate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An allowlist that routes unrecognized labels to a person fails closed, which is the more conservative default.
statements.explanation: When the machine cannot classify, the safe fallback is to ask a human.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A flag from the allowlist design proves the data is sensitive.
statements.explanation: It shows only that the label was not recognized.

questions.source: What a validator refuses vs what a person judges
questions.stem: A designer wants an automated check on governance records, such as a list of banned phrases for the owner and evaluation lines. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether an evaluation line describes an adequate test is a judgment for a person.
statements.explanation: Adequacy depends on the system and the harm, which strings cannot encode.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A numeric limit such as a maximum retention period belongs in code, because a validator can enforce it exactly.
statements.explanation: A range is something a validator can check exactly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A banned-phrase list reliably detects weak owner lines.
statements.explanation: Minor rewording passes while saying the same thing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An LLM judge scoring an owner line as adequate replaces the named person's acceptance of the role.
statements.explanation: A score cannot stand in for the person accepting responsibility.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A validator that states narrowly what it checks is more honest than one implying it assesses quality.
statements.explanation: Overstated validators invite trust beyond what was tested.

questions.stem: A validator marks this record "ready-for-human-review": owner "everyone", purpose "help", approver "manager", evaluation "looks fine", incident contact "team", retention 99999 days. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "everyone" in the owner field is a group label, not an accountable person.
statements.explanation: No individual has accepted responsibility.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The vague lines are tested against the real world by a person, not by the validator.
statements.explanation: Meaning and sufficiency need human judgment.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A retention of 99999 days works as a meaningful stated retention period.
statements.explanation: It is effectively unlimited retention, which defeats the purpose of stating a period.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A purpose of "help" bounds the use of the system clearly.
statements.explanation: It excludes nothing, so no later use can be called out of scope.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The record shows that a presence-and-shape check is not evidence of adequate governance.
statements.explanation: The record is complete yet weak, so the status cannot certify quality.

questions.source: Truthy and falsy in a presence check
questions.stem: A validator decides a field is missing with the test `not record.get(field)`. One record sets retention_days to 0 as a deliberate design choice, and a second record leaves out a key entirely. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 0 is falsy in Python, so this test reports retention_days as missing.
statements.explanation: A falsy value is treated the same as an absent one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A string made of spaces is falsy and is reported as missing.
statements.explanation: A non-empty string is truthy even when it holds only whitespace.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A key that is absent is skipped, because the lookup returns a default that is ignored.
statements.explanation: The default is falsy, so the absent key is reported as missing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Testing explicitly for a missing value, rather than for falsiness, separates an absent value from a legitimate zero.
statements.explanation: An explicit missing-value test does not treat 0 as absent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A falsiness test distinguishes a deliberate zero from an absent value.
statements.explanation: It treats both the same.

questions.source: isinstance vs exact type; bool is a subclass of int
questions.stem: A function validates a retention-day count with `isinstance(d, int) and d >= 0`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Python, bool is a subclass of int.
statements.explanation: That is why True behaves as 1 in arithmetic.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An exact type test such as `type(d) is int` rejects True.
statements.explanation: type(True) is bool, which is not int.

statements.label: C
statements.text: isinstance(30.0, int) evaluates to True.
statements.explanation: 30.0 is a float, not an int.

statements.label: D
statements.text: isinstance(True, int) evaluates to True.
statements.explanation: A subclass instance passes an isinstance test for its parent class.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The function rejects 0 because zero is falsy.
statements.explanation: The function tests a type and a sign, not truthiness, so 0 passes.

questions.source: Test-first; checking a suite with wrong versions
questions.stem: A developer writes tests for a retention validator before asking an assistant to implement it. Two deliberately wrong versions exist: one accepts any value for which isinstance(d, int) is true, and one treats a falsy value as missing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test expecting True to be rejected tells the correct version from the isinstance version.
statements.explanation: The isinstance version accepts True because bool is a subclass of int.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Running the suite against deliberately wrong versions shows whether the suite can tell right from wrong.
statements.explanation: A suite that passes wrong versions is too weak.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A suite of a normal case plus an empty-record case, and nothing else, catches both wrong versions.
statements.explanation: Both wrong versions still pass those two cases.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A passing suite shows the implementation is correct for inputs the suite did not exercise.
statements.explanation: Tests demonstrate only the behavior they exercise.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tests written by a person from a specification before seeing the code capture that person's intent independently.
statements.explanation: They are not shaped by what the implementation happens to do.

questions.stem: A reviewer words claims in a validation write-up so that each claim is no stronger than its evidence. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Inspecting the stores the team controls supports claims about those stores.
statements.explanation: Evidence covers the stores that were actually examined.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Test coverage bounds a claim, because untested cases stay unknown.
statements.explanation: A passing suite speaks only for the cases it ran.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A labeled test report sent to the incident contact and acknowledged within the stated time is evidence the route works.
statements.explanation: The route was exercised, not just listed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reading a provider's documentation that says logs are deleted supports "we verified deletion at the provider".
statements.explanation: Documentation is the provider's claim; verification needs inspection.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "The validator confirmed the workflow is safe" is worded no stronger than a script run supports.
statements.explanation: The script checked presence and shape; it did not establish safety.

questions.stem: An assistant approved to summarize public course notes is later pointed at student-submitted essays. Its register purpose field reads "use AI". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The purpose field is decoration because a validator is unable to judge it.
statements.explanation: The field forces the team to state a boundary a person can test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using the assistant on a different kind of data is a change of scope that triggers re-review.
statements.explanation: New data and new affected people need a fresh decision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An unchanged model and prompt mean an unchanged risk profile.
statements.explanation: Risk depends on the data, the people affected and the consequences.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A broad purpose is preferable because it avoids re-review when uses change.
statements.explanation: A broad purpose excludes nothing, so scope creep goes unnoticed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A purpose statement gives a boundary that people can later check uses against.
statements.explanation: The value of the field is in stating a limit.

questions.stem: A register states "retention: 30 days" for user prompts. Prompts also appear in a nightly backup kept 90 days, an e-mailed weekly report and a model provider's service logs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stated retention number shows that deletion happened at that time.
statements.explanation: A number states policy for a store; it is not evidence of deletion.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deleting a prompt from the application log removes summaries derived from it.
statements.explanation: Derived artifacts live in other stores and may still reveal the source.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A prompt copied into a nightly backup follows the backup's own retention period.
statements.explanation: The backup's lifetime is set by its own schedule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A deletion test inserts a labeled test record, runs the lifecycle and inspects the stores the team controls.
statements.explanation: Inspecting copies is how deletion is verified.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retention covers the whole lifecycle of the data, including backups, exports and provider copies.
statements.explanation: A policy about one store does not govern the others.

questions.stem: A design document sets retention_days to 0 for a workflow that handles customer messages that go to an external model provider. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Zero can mean delete right after the task, do not persist application data, or keep a de-identified record as evidence.
statements.explanation: The number does not say which is intended, so the document needs to.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Zero retention in the company's own systems makes the provider's terms irrelevant.
statements.explanation: The provider still processes the data under its own terms.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The register should record the provider's retention separately from the company's own.
statements.explanation: Different parties hold different copies under different rules.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A presence check based on falsiness wrongly reports a zero as missing.
statements.explanation: 0 is falsy, so a presence test needs to check for absence instead.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A stated zero is evidence that no copies exist.
statements.explanation: A stated value is a design intent; copies can exist regardless.

questions.stem: A team deletes a customer's row from its application database after a deletion request. The customer's data also fed a vector index of embeddings, a weekly summary, a log of hashed e-mail addresses and a backup. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An embedding in a vector index holds no information from its source once it is embedded.
statements.explanation: Embeddings are derived data that can still carry information about the source.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Stores the team is unable to verify, such as provider systems and backups, are listed as open rather than assumed clean.
statements.explanation: Unexamined copies stay unknown.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Removed from this table" supports the claim "erased everywhere".
statements.explanation: The claim needs every copy and derivative to be accounted for.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A hashed identifier counts as a derived copy of a record that can be matched back to a person.
statements.explanation: A hash used for matching is still linked to a person; treat it as a copy needing a decision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Removing a withdrawn participant's quotation from the published summary completes the withdrawal.
statements.explanation: The words may remain in an index, an evaluation set and a backup.

questions.stem: A team compares three ways to log an AI agent's actions: keep full prompts and outputs indefinitely, keep nothing, or keep a minimal audit record. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Keeping nothing is the privacy-safest option and needs no further justification.
statements.explanation: It trades privacy for the loss of accountability and needs justification.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Keeping no trace leaves no way to reconstruct what the agent did after an incident.
statements.explanation: Without a record, review and recourse are not possible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Keeping full prompts and outputs indefinitely creates its own exposure.
statements.explanation: Retained content is a target for leaks and misuse.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A minimal audit record should hold the full prompt and output text so reviewers see everything.
statements.explanation: A minimal record holds identifiers and references, not the content.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A minimal record can hold an operation ID, the policy decision taken, references to evidence stored elsewhere and an error category.
statements.explanation: References support review without duplicating sensitive data.

questions.stem: Two LLM agents score the same on the same evaluation set. Agent A reads public notes and writes a local draft that a person publishes. Agent B reads internal HR records, publishes straight to an external site and keeps its inputs for a long time. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An evaluation score measures performance on a test set, not exposure or consequence.
statements.explanation: Risk also depends on data, audience and what the agent can do.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reversibility describes how often an action is repeated.
statements.explanation: Reversibility describes how hard an action is to undo.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Saving a draft in a private workspace is easier to undo than publishing to an indexed public website.
statements.explanation: A public, indexed copy is hard to recall.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Action surface is the set of systems and audiences an agent's actions can reach.
statements.explanation: Agent B has a larger action surface than Agent A.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Identical scores mean the two agents need identical governance.
statements.explanation: Different data and different consequences call for different controls.

questions.source: Error types and who bears them
questions.stem: Two summarizers make the same number of deadline errors. Summarizer X states a deadline its sources do not support. Summarizer Y leaves the deadline out when its sources conflict. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting error types separately shows who bears each kind of error.
statements.explanation: Splitting by direction and consequence exposes who is affected.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Equal accuracy means the two kinds of error cost the same to the people affected.
statements.explanation: A false statement and an omission harm different people differently.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A false positive and a false negative can fall on different people.
statements.explanation: Who bears an error depends on the direction of the error.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Leaving out a deadline when sources conflict is an abstention that moves the checking work to the reader.
statements.explanation: The error exists but is visible to the reader.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Stating a deadline the sources do not support is a fabrication, often called a hallucination.
statements.explanation: The output asserts something unsupported by the evidence.

questions.source: Base rate, PPV and fairness criteria
questions.stem: A classifier is applied to two groups with different base rates of true positives. Its true positive rate and false positive rate are the same for both groups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal true and false positive rates guarantee equal positive predictive value across the groups.
statements.explanation: Differing base rates change positive predictive value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Positive predictive value depends on the base rate as well as on the error rates.
statements.explanation: With a lower base rate, a larger share of positive predictions are false.

statements.label: C
statements.text: True positive rate is the share of positive predictions that are correct.
statements.explanation: That is positive predictive value; true positive rate is the share of actual positives found.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Fairness criteria can conflict, so choosing one is a value decision.
statements.explanation: Numbers cannot say which definition of fair a society should adopt.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The data alone will identify the correct fairness definition.
statements.explanation: The choice reflects values and context.

questions.stem: A company reports that its resume-ranking LLM agrees with past hiring decisions on an evaluation set built from people who were hired. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Historical labels can carry the bias of earlier decisions into the model.
statements.explanation: A model trained or checked against past outcomes reproduces their pattern.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A false negative here is a qualified applicant who is ranked low.
statements.explanation: A false negative is a real positive that the tool misses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A set built from hired people contains no rejected candidates, so false negatives are invisible.
statements.explanation: Qualified people who were passed over never appear.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Agreement with past decisions measures consistency with history, not whether those decisions were good.
statements.explanation: The labels are only as sound as the process that produced them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overall agreement shows who bears the false positives.
statements.explanation: A single aggregate hides who is affected.

questions.source: Generic risk vs concrete harm; matched mitigation
questions.stem: A risk register for an LLM tool contains the entry "There may be bias or privacy concerns." Another entry says a student relies on a summary with the wrong deadline and misses the real one. A third lists, for retained health-question logs, the mitigation "weekly test of answer accuracy". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A weekly accuracy test mitigates the harm of retained logs being exposed.
statements.explanation: Accuracy testing addresses a different harm from exposure of stored data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A concrete harm lets a team choose a signal, a threshold and an owner.
statements.explanation: Specific harm points to what to measure and who should respond.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "There may be bias or privacy concerns" is a generic risk statement.
statements.explanation: It names no affected person, event or path.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A concrete harm description names the model's architecture rather than the affected person.
statements.explanation: A concrete harm names who is harmed, what happens and how.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A mitigation is matched to a harm when it reduces that harm's likelihood or severity.
statements.explanation: Matching is judged against the named harm.

questions.stem: A team plans to consult people affected by a new AI workflow and tries an LLM that role-plays an affected student. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Replies from an LLM role-playing a student are simulated responses, not evidence of what real people think.
statements.explanation: The model produces plausible text, often agreeable, with no stake in the outcome.

statements.label: B
