statements.text: If the second sort were unstable, the two-pass approach would still keep salary order inside each department.
statements.explanation: An unstable sort may reorder equal departments, so a single combined key would be needed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Stable" here means the sort returns the same output when run on different inputs.
statements.explanation: Stability is about ties within one input.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Stable" here means the sort does not crash on large lists.
statements.explanation: It describes tie order, not robustness.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Python's sorted keeps the original relative order of items whose keys are equal.
statements.explanation: Equal keys keep their earlier order.

questions.stem: A vendor release note says an endpoint of the Claude API is "stable", and a developer wants to build a client on it. Which statements about this sense of "stable" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Stable" in an API and "stable" in a sort name the same property.
statements.explanation: Tie order versus compatibility.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A stable API returns the same response time on each call.
statements.explanation: Latency is a different property.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pinning a dated model snapshot is a way to keep model behaviour steady between releases.
statements.explanation: A pinned snapshot does not change under the client.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stable API keeps its documented fields and behaviour compatible across versions so existing clients keep working.
statements.explanation: Stable means compatibility.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A stable endpoint means the model returns identical text for repeated calls.
statements.explanation: Output variation comes from sampling, not API stability.

questions.stem: A Python function updates a config file by writing to a temporary file in the same folder and then calling os.replace to put it over the real file. A reader may open the config at any moment. Which statements about "atomic" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Opening the config in "w" mode and writing it directly is atomic because Python does it in one call.
statements.explanation: A reader can see a truncated or half-written file.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An atomic update either completes in full or leaves no visible change to other readers.
statements.explanation: No partial state is visible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An atomic write is seen by readers as either the old file or the new file, never a mixture.
statements.explanation: Readers never see a partial file.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In planning, an "atomic task" means a small step that can be checked alone, which is a different sense from an atomic write.
statements.explanation: Two senses of the same word.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing a temp file and then os.replace onto the target is a common way to get an atomic file update on one filesystem.
statements.explanation: The replace step is a single rename.

questions.stem: A user tells Claude Code: "Make each commit atomic." The branch currently has one commit that fixes a bug and renames three modules. Which statements are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The mixed bug-fix and rename commit already satisfies the request.
statements.explanation: It should be split into a fix commit and a rename commit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An atomic commit is applied by git as a database transaction that rolls back on failure.
statements.explanation: That is the database sense, not the git sense.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Atomic commits make review and revert easier because each can be undone on its own.
statements.explanation: Separate changes revert separately.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In git, an atomic commit holds one logical change.
statements.explanation: One change per commit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An atomic commit has the fewest lines possible.
statements.explanation: Size is not the test; one logical change is.

questions.stem: A Python tool returns a dictionary that includes a datetime value, and the result must be sent back to Claude as a tool_result. Which statements about "serializable" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tool_result accepts a Python dict object directly without conversion.
statements.explanation: Content is text or blocks, so convert first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Serializable here means convertible to a text or byte format such as JSON and back.
statements.explanation: This is the data sense.

statements.label: C
statements.text: json.dumps converts a datetime object without any extra handling.
statements.explanation: It raises TypeError.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing a default= function to json.dumps is one way to convert types it cannot handle.
statements.explanation: The function is called for unknown types.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Serializable isolation in a database is the same property as an object being JSON-serializable.
statements.explanation: Different meaning.

questions.stem: Two database transactions each read an account balance of 100, check that a withdrawal of 80 is allowed, and then subtract 80. The team wants only one to succeed. Which statements about "serializable" isolation are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Serializable isolation means each transaction's rows can be written to JSON.
statements.explanation: Wrong sense.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Serializable isolation works because Python's GIL runs the transactions on one thread.
statements.explanation: The database enforces it, not the interpreter.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A weaker isolation level can let both transactions read 100 and both subtract, which is a lost update.
statements.explanation: This is the check-then-act race.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Serializable isolation makes the outcome match some order of running the transactions one after another.
statements.explanation: That is the definition.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Under serializable isolation the two withdrawals cannot both commit from the same starting balance of 100.
statements.explanation: One would abort or see the updated balance.

questions.stem: A developer calls the Claude API with the same long system prompt and tool definitions on each request and wants lower cost and latency. Which statements about prompt caching are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Prompt caching reuses processing of an unchanged prompt prefix.
statements.explanation: The prefix is the cached part.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Prompt caching stores Claude's earlier answers and returns them when the same question repeats.
statements.explanation: It caches input processing, not answers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Changing a sentence near the start of the prefix breaks reuse for the text after it.
statements.explanation: The cache matches from the beginning.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Prompt caching teaches the model the cached text, as fine-tuning does.
statements.explanation: Weights are not changed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Putting the changing user text before the system prompt helps produce cache hits.
statements.explanation: Stable content goes first.

questions.stem: A Python function ask(question) calls Claude and is decorated with functools.lru_cache. The same question is asked twice with temperature 1. Which statements about this "cache" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Arguments to an lru_cache function need to be hashable, so passing a list raises TypeError.
statements.explanation: Hashing is how entries are keyed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A cached function that depends on the current time or on external data can return stale values.
statements.explanation: The cache does not know the world changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: lru_cache returns the stored result for the same arguments without running the function body again.
statements.explanation: Second call skips the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because temperature is 1, the second call returns a fresh, different answer.
statements.explanation: The cached answer is returned.

statements.label: E
statements.text: lru_cache and API prompt caching are the same mechanism.
statements.explanation: One is in your process, one is on the provider side.

questions.stem: A user told Claude Code a rule an hour ago and Claude now ignores it. The session is very long. Which statements about "context" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Context is the tokens the model reads for a request, including earlier turns kept in the conversation.
statements.explanation: Context is the input.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fact stated once in the conversation is visible to the model only while it is still inside the window.
statements.explanation: Once outside the window it is not seen.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A larger context window makes the model learn the rule permanently.
statements.explanation: The window is not learning.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When a conversation exceeds the context window, older content can be dropped or summarised, so the rule may no longer be seen.
statements.explanation: Hence the lapse.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Moving the rule into CLAUDE.md puts it in context at the start of each session.
statements.explanation: Memory files are loaded at session start.

questions.stem: A user asks Claude to "give the model more context" so a Python bug is diagnosed correctly. Which statements correctly unpack this request? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding context to a prompt changes the model's weights.
statements.explanation: It changes the input only.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Saying "you remember our earlier chats" supplies context from them even when they are not included.
statements.explanation: Absent text is not visible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pasting a whole log is as exact as naming the failing section, since the model reads all of it.
statements.explanation: Irrelevant text can crowd out the relevant lines.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding the failing file contents, the error text and the goal to the prompt adds context.
statements.explanation: Context is what is in the prompt.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In "context window", context is a limit measured in tokens.
statements.explanation: Window size is counted in tokens.

questions.stem: A user says to Claude Code: "Remember that we use pytest, so you know it next week." Nothing else is configured. Which statements about "memory" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A CLAUDE.md file is discarded when the session that read it ends.
statements.explanation: The file stays on disk and is read again next session.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Python list of messages in RAM survives a restart of the script.
statements.explanation: Process memory is lost on exit.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Model weights update after each chat so the model remembers the user.
statements.explanation: Weights are fixed at inference.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Saying "remember this" to Claude Code writes it to durable storage on its own.
statements.explanation: Nothing is saved unless a file or store is written.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Conversation history inside one session is context, not durable memory across sessions.
statements.explanation: It disappears when the session ends.

questions.stem: A developer builds a Python agent for a support desk and wants it to recall customer preferences from last month. Which statements about "memory" in this design are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Appending notes to a JSON file that the agent reads at start is a memory store.
statements.explanation: Notes persist outside the model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fine-tuning after each chat is the usual way to give an agent memory of one user.
statements.explanation: It is slow, costly and not per-user.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The API server stores your message list between calls, so the code need not resend it.
statements.explanation: The Messages API is stateless.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Retrieving past notes into the prompt changes the model's weights so it remembers the customer.
statements.explanation: Retrieval changes the input, not the weights.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The message list sent in each API call is short-term conversation state that the code resends.
statements.explanation: The code carries the state.

questions.stem: A Python script calls Claude to classify a ticket, calls Claude again to draft a reply, and then sends the email, in that fixed order every run. Which statements are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fixed-path workflow is easier to test because the sequence of steps is predictable.
statements.explanation: Fewer paths to cover.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Wrapping the three calls in a function named agent makes it an agent.
statements.explanation: A name does not give it a decision loop.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A step in a workflow can call Claude with a prompt, and the program is still a workflow.
statements.explanation: Model calls inside fixed steps are allowed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is a workflow because code fixes the steps.
statements.explanation: Path set in advance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A system where Claude picks among tools and loops until it judges the task done is an agent.
statements.explanation: The model chooses the path.

questions.stem: A team must handle support requests where the number and kind of steps differ per request, and one proposal uses an agent loop while another uses a fixed pipeline. Which statements are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Work whose steps cannot be listed in advance fits an agent loop.
statements.explanation: The model decides the next step.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using an agent for a fixed three-step pipeline adds cost and variability for no gain.
statements.explanation: Over-engineering.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An agent loop needs no stop condition because the model decides when to end.
statements.explanation: A step or time limit is still set.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Work with the same steps in the same order each run needs an agent loop, since a loop adapts.
statements.explanation: A fixed path fits a workflow.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Switching from a workflow to an agent makes the outputs deterministic.
statements.explanation: It adds run-time variability.

questions.stem: A team uses Claude Code and wants to add capabilities. They are comparing a tool with a skill. Which statements are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A skill is an API function that returns data from an external service.
statements.explanation: That describes a tool.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tool_use block is how Claude requests a call to a tool.
statements.explanation: Request side of the exchange.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A skill is a packaged set of instructions, with optional scripts, that Claude loads when relevant.
statements.explanation: Skills guide.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tool is a callable function with a schema that Claude can invoke to take an action.
statements.explanation: Tools act.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Installing a skill gives Claude a permission it did not have.
statements.explanation: Permissions are set separately.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to follow its code-review checklist and also to look up ticket status in an internal ticket database. Which statements about choosing a skill or a tool are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A skill that is only text can read the ticket database without any tool.
statements.explanation: Reading data takes a callable action.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A skill can tell Claude how and when to use a tool.
statements.explanation: Instructions can reference tools.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Looking up ticket status needs a tool, for example one exposed by an MCP server.
statements.explanation: It requires an action.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Writing the checklist as a tool with a schema is the right form for text guidance.
statements.explanation: A tool is for action, not guidance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The checklist is instructions, so it fits a skill or CLAUDE.md.
statements.explanation: Text guidance.

questions.stem: A Python program calls the Anthropic Messages API with a system parameter and a messages list. Which statements about "prompt" and "system prompt" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Prompt means only the text of the latest user message.
statements.explanation: Prompt can mean the whole input.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The system parameter holds standing instructions such as role and rules for the conversation.
statements.explanation: System prompt is standing text.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rule placed in the system prompt is enforced by the API, so the model obeys it.
statements.explanation: It guides, it does not guarantee.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A user message in messages is treated as part of the system prompt.
statements.explanation: The system prompt is the separate system parameter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The system prompt is stored by the model and reused in other conversations.
statements.explanation: It is sent with each request.

questions.stem: A developer builds a Python app that pastes retrieved web pages into Claude's input, and one page contains the text "ignore your rules". Which statements about where to place text are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A system-prompt rule reduces the chance that pasted instructions change behaviour, so checks outside the prompt are still needed.
statements.explanation: Prompts are not enforcement.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Untrusted text belongs in the user turn, clearly delimited and labelled as data.
statements.explanation: Delimiting reduces confusion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Putting retrieved text in the system parameter would give any instructions in it standing authority.
statements.explanation: Placement affects weight.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Putting retrieved text in the system parameter is a safe way to make Claude treat it as data.
statements.explanation: It does the opposite.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The system prompt is hidden from the model's view of the conversation.
statements.explanation: The model reads it.

questions.stem: Claude's summary of a codebase cites a function parse_header that does not exist in the repository. Which statements about "hallucination" and "error" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A hallucination is fluent output that states something not supported by the source or the facts.
statements.explanation: The cited function is unsupported.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An exception such as a 404 returned in a tool_result is an error, not a hallucination.
statements.explanation: The tool reports it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A hallucinated claim can be checked by searching the repository for the named function.
statements.explanation: Check against the source.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A syntax error in generated Python is a hallucination.
statements.explanation: It is an error caught by the interpreter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking Claude "are you sure?" does not by itself verify a claim; a check against the repository does.
statements.explanation: Self-confirmation is not independent evidence.

questions.stem: An agent reports "I updated config.yaml" but the file is unchanged, and another run of the agent hit a PermissionError from a write tool. Which statements are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A PermissionError is fixed by telling the agent in the prompt to be more careful, with no change to permissions.
statements.explanation: A permission fault is fixed by scope or path.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Both problems are fixed by raising the temperature.
statements.explanation: Sampling does not cause either.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A claimed update with no change on disk is a claim/code mismatch, a fabricated report.
statements.explanation: The claim lacks evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A PermissionError counts as a hallucination because the model did not predict it.
statements.explanation: A tool reported a real error.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Running git diff or listing the file is a check that settles the first claim.
statements.explanation: Evidence beats assertion.

questions.stem: A team has a pytest suite for a function that parses model output into a dict and also has 200 graded questions for judging answer quality. Which statements about "test" and "evaluation" are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An eval compares the output with one fixed expected string exactly.
statements.explanation: That is a test; evals score varying output.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A passing pytest suite shows the answer quality is good.
statements.explanation: It only checks the code's fixed expectations.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Running the evals removes the need for tests on the parsing code.
statements.explanation: They check different things.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An eval produces a single pass or fail for the whole run, as a test does.
statements.explanation: Evals usually give scores or rates.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test checks a fixed expectation with a pass or fail result, such as the parser returning the expected dict.
statements.explanation: Test = fixed pass/fail.

questions.stem: A user asks Claude Code: "Evaluate my prompt change." Which statements about writing an exact instruction and judging the result are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A held-out set not used while editing the prompt gives a fairer estimate of performance on new inputs.
statements.explanation: Avoids tuning to the cases.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Run pytest" evaluates the quality of the prompt.
statements.explanation: Pytest checks fixed expectations of code.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using the same cases and the same scoring for both prompts makes the comparison fair.
statements.explanation: Only the prompt differs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Tuning the prompt on the eval cases and then reporting those scores shows how it will do on new inputs.
statements.explanation: That is overfitting to the cases.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Run the 200-case eval on the old and new prompt and report both scores" is an exact instruction.
statements.explanation: Names cases, versions and output.

questions.stem: A developer writes a Python MCP server with FastMCP that exposes a search function, and Claude Desktop connects to it. Which statements about "server" and "client" in MCP are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The client is the host application, such as Claude Desktop or Claude Code, that connects to servers and relays tool calls.
statements.explanation: Client consumes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The model's weights run inside the MCP server.
statements.explanation: The model is separate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One server can be connected to by more than one client application, such as Claude Desktop and Claude Code.
statements.explanation: The server is a separate process that clients connect to.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The server exposes capabilities such as tools, resources and prompts.
statements.explanation: Server offers.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An MCP server can run locally on the user's machine and talk over stdio.
statements.explanation: Local servers are common.

questions.stem: A Python MCP server exposes a delete_file tool, and the team asks where to put controls. Which statements about MCP roles are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A local stdio script is not an MCP server, since "server" means a remote machine.
statements.explanation: Server is a role, not a location.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The server chooses which of the client's tools to run.
statements.explanation: The client side, with the model, chooses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A path allowlist inside the server adds a second control on what the tool can touch.
statements.explanation: Defence in two places.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An approval gate is usually placed in the client or host, before the tool call is sent.
statements.explanation: The host asks the user.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The client sends a tools/call request and the server returns the result.
statements.explanation: Request and response.

questions.stem: A bug report says "Claude deleted the file". The team wants to separate model from agent. Which statements are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Switching to a larger model changes a chat system into an agent.
statements.explanation: Tools and a loop make an agent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The word "Claude" names only the model, so a report need not say which layer acted.
statements.explanation: It can name the model or a product that wraps it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Fine-tuning a model produces an agent.
statements.explanation: Fine-tuning changes weights, not tools.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An agent is a model combined with tools, instructions and a loop.
statements.explanation: Agent adds action.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A model has tool access built in, so it can run commands by itself.
statements.explanation: A model only produces tokens; tools come from the harness.

questions.stem: A Claude Code run deleted a file the user wanted to keep, and the team is deciding what to change. Which statements about model and agent are true? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing the model version alone fixes the issue regardless of permission settings.
statements.explanation: The permission still allows delete.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The model proposed the tool call and the harness executed it.
statements.explanation: Proposal versus execution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The deletion was carried out by the model's weights.
statements.explanation: Weights only produce tokens.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the permission scope allowed delete, the agent's configuration, not the model alone, decided what could run.
statements.explanation: Scope sets what can happen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A good report names the model version and the tool and permission configuration.
statements.explanation: Both layers matter.
